text:
(Bangkok) – Thai authorities should halt the imminent deportation of 26 ethnic Karen villagers from Phetchaburi province to Myanmar and release them from immigration detention, Human Rights Watch said today.

On August 10, 2026, district and forestry officials along with the Thai military raided the Karen community in Ban Pa Deng village in Phetchaburi province’s Kaeng Krachan National Park, targeting those without proof of Thai citizenship. The authorities arrested twenty-eight villagers, including eight children and two pregnant women, and placed them in the custody of the Phetchaburi provincial immigration office. Two villagers were later released after local officials verified their residence registration records. The immigration office then transferred the remaining 26 villagers to the Suan Phlu Immigration Detention Center in Bangkok to prosecute them on immigration charges and deport them to Myanmar.

“Deporting ethnic Karen villagers to Myanmar would put them at risk of grave danger,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “Thai authorities should work with the community to ensure access to their ancestral lands for their livelihood.”

Since the February 2021 coup, Myanmar’s military junta has carried out a nationwide campaign of mass killings, torture, arbitrary arrests, and unlawful attacks that amount to crimes against humanity and war crimes. More than two million people have been internally displaced and over 100,000 refugees have fled to neighboring countries.

In the face of recent escalating fighting in Myanmar, Thai authorities have summarily determined that undocumented Karen in the Kaeng Krachan National Park, including local villagers, are “illegal immigrants,” community leaders told Human Rights Watch. Such classification means they are vulnerable to arrest and deportation to Myanmar. Residents of Ban Pa Deng village said that at least 10 villagers remain unaccounted for after Thai authorities deported them to Myanmar about two months ago.

Deporting the 26 Karen villagers to Myanmar could violate Thailand’s obligations as a party to the United Nations Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment as well as the customary international law principle prohibiting refoulement, the forcible return of anyone to a place where they would face a genuine risk of persecution, torture or other ill-treatment, or a threat to their life. In addition, Thailand’s Prevention and Suppression of Torture and Enforced Disappearance Act prohibits deportation when there is a substantial risk of torture or ill-treatment.

Ethnic Karen people have lived in both Thailand and Myanmar for generations, including in the jungle in Phetchaburi and Prachuap Khiri Khan provinces, long before the establishment of the Kaeng Krachan National Park. Hundreds of thousands of Karen in Thailand have colored identification cards, meaning they are a recognized hilltribe group in Thailand, but others who arrived in Thailand more recently have no legal status. Karen frequently travel between their communities across the Thailand-Myanmar border, Human Rights Watch said.

In 2021, the UNESCO World Heritage Committee placed the Kaeng Krachan Forest Complex on the World Heritage List, leading the Thai authorities to prohibit human settlement, including of Karen people, in the Kaeng Krachan National Park. This decision was made despite concerns raised by UN human rights experts, the National Human Rights Commission of Thailand, and Indigenous groups about the ancestral land rights of ethnic Karen.

The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous People, a nonbinding international instrument, provides in article 26(2) that “Indigenous peoples have the right to own, use, develop and control the lands, territories and resources that they possess by reason of traditional ownership or other traditional occupation or use.” The UN human rights experts raised the lack of “good faith consultations with the [Karen] community allowing them to participate in the UNESCO nomination process.”

Over the past three decades, Thai authorities have pressured Karen villagers to leave their homes in the Kaeng Krachan National Park, at times violently, including by raiding their villages, burning their farms and properties, and forcibly relocating them. The relocation sites set up by Thai authorities for the Karen are inadequate and unsuitable for their traditional farming, Human Rights Watch said. In August 2022, Kaeng Krahan National Park officials were indicted in relation to the enforced disappearance of the Karen leader and human rights defender Ban Pa Deng Porlajee “Billy” Rakchongcharoen in April 2014. In September 2023, they were acquitted of murder based on lack of evidence.

“Ahead of the UN Human Rights Council’s review of Thailand’s human rights record in November, the Thai government should immediately end its abusive treatment of ethnic Karen in the Kaeng Krachan National Park,” Pearson said. “Concerned governments and UN agencies should press the Thai government to ensure that the fundamental rights of Karen are respected and protected.”

title: State health inspections of ICE detention facilities halted by Legislature - Sacramento Bee

text:
A bill authorizing the California Department of Public Health to inspect residential detention facilities was halted in an Assembly hearing Thursday.

Senate Bill 995, known as the Masuma Khan Justice Act, would create a uniform statewide system to regulate heating, ventilation, air, water and electrical systems in detention centers. It would also mandate adherence to occupational safety and health regulations in an effort to address reported deficiencies in access to mental health and medical care.

The measure is named after Masuma Khan, a 65-year-old resident of Altadena, California. During an April hearing in the Senate Standing Committee on Health, bill author state Sen. Sasha Pérez, D-Alhambra, said Khan was held for over a month in a cold facility without access to warm clothing, edible food, clean drinking water or the medications she needed.

“SB 995 is grounded in a simple principle,” Pérez said. “If detention facilities operate in California, they must meet California’s standards for safety, dignity and human rights.”

Khan has lived in the U.S. since 1997 with her daughter and husband, both American citizens. Though she has no criminal record, Khan was detained at California City Detention Center after a routine immigration check-in in downtown Los Angeles. During a month in detention, Khan was denied access to necessary medications for hypothyroidism, high blood pressure and glaucoma, according to testimony by her daughter, Riya Khan.

“When I visited her one day, she was having shortness of breath, she couldn’t walk, her legs were so swollen and painful that they were bruising up and she was shaking,” Khan said in an interview with The Sacramento Bee. “That scared me because I was afraid my mom was going to die in that place when she’s done nothing wrong.”

Riya Khan said those held in the facility were served moldy, insect-infested bread, drank dirty water and lived in below-freezing conditions. The LED floodlights outside the center are left on all night, she said, and guards slam doors at all hours, keeping detainees awake.

“This is unacceptable and disgusting,” Riya Khan said. “We have people dying at a record rate … There is a complete and utter disregard for human lives at this point. And this can be prevented by having certain rules and regulations in place.”

After seeing the conditions in which her mother was held, Khan said she “reached out to anyone and everyone” — news organizations, social media creators and legislators like Pérez. According to Pérez, she pledged to author the bill last fall after hearing what Masuma Khan went through.

“Masuma looked at me at one point and said, ‘If these facilities are located in California and you’re a California state senator, why would you not be able to … do something about this?’” Pérez said in an interview with The Bee. “I felt like the point she made in that moment was very accurate. Why should we not be able to do anything? Why haven’t we done more?”

Pushback over redundancy

While the bill received unanimous support in Senate votes and during committee hearings in both chambers, some said its provisions may have been duplicative of existing law.

“We have concerns with some of the provisions in the bill that we believe would create … duplicative oversight for health facilities that are already licensed and regulated under some of the most stringent regulations in the nation,” said Leah Barros on behalf of the California Hospital Association.

Barros said there were worries that permitting state-run health inspections on federally overseen detention facilities may invite legal challenges. Additionally, the bill would group private detention facilities with licensed behavioral health facilities already governed by strict state operating guidelines.

“While SB 995 addresses a serious issue, its significant costs and lengthy implementation timeline raised concerns about whether the proposal, as written, would translate into timely, meaningful protections for the people it was intended to help,” Wicks said in a written statement to The Bee.

Loading…

Some were opposed to the inclusion of county juvenile facilities in the definition of “involuntary residential facility” in the bill. At an Assembly Health Committee hearing in June, Chief Probation Officers of California Legislative Director Danielle Sanchez said these facilities are already subjected to judicious inspection and would not benefit from additional oversight.

“Because there’s an existing framework, adding duplication and layering a new one … actually does more harm than good in carrying out the state framework that has been established,” Sanchez said in testimony.

Pérez maintained that the state has the authority to implement the legislation outlined in the bill. She referenced a bill passed in 2024 that would allow county-level health inspections of detention facilities. Though the bill’s language is similar to SB 995, it is limited by county-specific politics, according to Pérez.

“[The 2024] bill was very powerful and innovative,” Pérez said. “But I don’t think we considered what would happen if a privately run immigration detention facility needed to be investigated and the county itself, the board of supervisors, did not want to initiate the investigation. And that’s what’s happened.”

According to Pérez, California City Detention Center is located in a conservative area whose county officials refused to initiate an investigation into the facility’s conditions. This made it difficult, she said, to hold elected officials accountable for Masuma Khan’s treatment while there.

“This is part of the reason why I believe, and will continue to argue, that the state needs to take over that oversight and accountability framework,” Pérez said. “This is a statewide issue, it is a national issue, and we can no longer just rely on these county agencies.”

The bill was halted by the Assembly Appropriations Committee along with dozens of other measures.

“I’m so heartbroken,” Pérez said. “We are moving past a moment where this is a partisan issue, and I think people are beginning to realize that these are human rights abuses that we need to take action around. I really hope there will be reconsideration here … I cannot think of a more urgent issue than this one.”

name: Litigation
title: Advance Parole Is No Longer a Safe Harbor From the Unlawful Presence Bars
description:
Practitioners evaluated a client's unlawful presence history by distinguishing between an advance parole authorized trip from other trips for purposes of § 212(a)(9)(B).
It also pointed to other provisions of the INA where Congress expressly addressed the consequences of departures under advance parole.
The Delcarmen-Lara decision requires a new analysis of how much unlawful presence a client has accrued before departing on advance parole.
What Practitioners Should Do Now Immigration practitioners should consider taking the following steps: Identify clients with outstanding advance parole documents.
And the lengthy processing time for Form I-131 advance parole applications — currently 23 months — has made applying for advance parole less desirable.
text:
The Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) overturned one of the more important interpretations of immigration law affecting adjustment of status applicants who have accrued unlawful presence. In Matter of Milagro Delcarmen-Lara, 29 I&N Dec. 830 (BIA 2026), decided Aug. 13, 2026, the BIA held that a trip outside the United States pursuant to a grant of advance parole is a “departure” for purposes of INA § 212(a)(9)(B)(i)(II). That statutory ground of inadmissibility governs the ten-year bar for unlawful presence that is triggered by a departure.

The Board expressly overruled Matter of Arrabally and Yerrabelly, 25 I&N Dec. 771 (BIA 2012), which for more than 14 years has provided protection to people who had accrued unlawful presence and traveled abroad on advance parole. The BIA has now held unequivocally that a departure from the United States pursuant to a grant of advance parole is a “departure” for purposes of § 212(a)(9)(B)(i)(II). While noncitizens may still travel on advance parole and, upon their return, be considered “inspected and admitted or paroled” for adjustment of status eligibility under INA § 245(a), their departure may trigger the unlawful presence bars. In addition, they may be refused entry to the United States by Customs and Border Protection (CBP) if they are found inadmissible under INA § 212(a)(9)(B).

What Arrabally and Yerrabelly Used to Provide

INA § 212(a)(9)(B) states that noncitizens become inadmissible after they accrue a certain amount of unlawful presence and then depart the United States. Before this recent BIA decision, the Arrabally and Yerrabelly decision provided an important exception. The BIA held that someone who temporarily left the United States pursuant to advance parole did not make the statutory “departure” that triggered the unlawful presence bar.

The BIA viewed an advance parole departure as fundamentally different from other departures because the government had authorized the person to leave temporarily and contemplated that they would return to continue pursuing adjustment of status. That interpretation became an important part of adjustment practice. Practitioners evaluated a client's unlawful presence history by distinguishing between an advance parole authorized trip from other trips for purposes of § 212(a)(9)(B). They had encouraged, for example, Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) and Temporary Protected Status (TPS) holders who had entered without inspection to leave under advance parole and create eligibility for adjustment of status should they become classified as an immediate relative (spouse, parent or child under 21 of a U.S. citizen).

The New Rule

Delcarmen-Lara holds that the word “departure” means what it ordinarily means: leaving the United States. The BIA relied heavily on the statutory text. Neither “depart” nor “departure” is defined in the INA, and the BIA found no language in § 212(a)(9)(B) creating an exception for departures pursuant to advance parole. It also pointed to other provisions of the INA where Congress expressly addressed the consequences of departures under advance parole. The BIA reasoned that Congress's decision to include such language elsewhere, but not in § 212(a)(9)(B), supported the conclusion that no advance parole exception should be implied here.

The BIA also pointed out that the Department of Homeland Security and the former Immigration and Naturalization Service had historically treated advance parole departures as potentially triggering the unlawful-presence bar before Arrabally. It noted that advance parole documents issued at that time had warned applicants that departure could result in inadmissibility.

Leaving the United States on advance parole is now a “departure” for purposes of triggering the INA § 212(a)(9)(B)(i)(II) ten-year unlawful presence bar.

Who Is Most Affected?

The Delcarmen-Lara decision requires a new analysis of how much unlawful presence a client has accrued before departing on advance parole. This demands a thorough understanding of the definition of unlawful presence as well as the exceptions. The decision specifically cites to § 212(a)(9)(B)(i)(II), which addresses the ten-year bar. But the same statutory definition of “departure” is relevant to the three-year bar in § 212(a)(9)(B)(i)(I). Thus, a person who accrued more than 180 days but less than one year of unlawful presence will trigger the three-year bar after departing on advance parole; a person who accrued one year or more will trigger the ten-year bar.

The BIA decision does not eliminate waiver possibilities under INA § 212(a)(9)(B)(v). Adjustment of status applicants can still file Form I-601, Application to Waive Grounds of Inadmissibility, to waive the three- or ten-year bars based on a showing of extreme hardship to a lawful permanent resident or U.S. citizen spouse or parent. Remember that the three or ten years can run while the person is residing in the United States after the reentry, pursuant to the BIA’s decision in Matter of Duarte-Gonzalez, 28 I&N Dec. 688 (BIA 2023).

This decision will likely mean that advance parole is no longer a viable option for those seeking to use it for adjustment of status eligibility. In addition, traveling under advance parole puts the noncitizen at risk of being refused entry to the United States altogether if they are subject to an inadmissibility ground. Rather than departing, triggering the ten-year bar, returning (hopefully), and then filing an I-601 waiver together with the adjustment application, they may opt instead to consular process. In those situations, they would file Form I-601A, Application for Provisional Unlawful Presence Waiver. After that is approved, they would depart for their immigrant visa interview. While the departure would trigger the ten-year unlawful presence bar, it would be waived at the immigrant visa application stage. Note that under the current administration, consular processing is an increasingly difficult option for those subject to either the travel ban for nationals from 39 countries or the immigrant visa suspension currently impacting 75 countries.

DACA recipients will be among the most affected, since those who had accrued unlawful presence before obtaining DACA had been able to use advance parole to travel abroad without triggering § 212(a)(9)(B). But it will also affect adjustment of status applicants, U-visa and T-visa holders, and others who are eligible for advance parole.

Note that USCIS policy since July 1, 2022, has been that TPS beneficiaries have traveled pursuant to “authorized travel” and not technically advance parole. However, it is likely that USCIS will take the position that the reasoning of Delcarmen-Lara applies equally to TPS beneficiaries traveling and “departing” pursuant to authorized travel.

Battered spouses and children require individualized analysis because INA § 212(a)(9)(B)(iii) contains a special provision concerning certain Violence Against Women Act (VAWA) self-petitioners. The unlawful presence bar does not apply if “there was a substantial connection between the battery or extreme cruelty…and the alien’s unlawful presence in the United States.”

Departure on Advance Parole Executes Removal Order

It has long been USCIS’s interpretation that those who travel on DACA advance parole execute any underlying removal order, although USCIS has taken the opposite approach for TPS-based advance parole and authorized travel. That interpretation appears to be unchanged by the Delcarmen-Lara decision. Therefore, the Delcarmen-Lara case should not have even come before the BIA because the underlying motion to reopen is likely to have been unnecessary.

The Delcarmen-Lara case arose out of the BIA’s consideration of a motion to reopen removal proceedings for a DACA beneficiary who had traveled under advance parole and sought to reopen her removal proceedings so she could apply to adjust status. The BIA denied reopening, and then separately made its findings on the statutory meaning of the term “departure” under § 212(a)(9)(B)(i)(II). But by departing pursuant to a grant of advance parole, the respondent in Delcarmen-Lara likely executed the removal order, leaving her free to pursue adjustment of status before USCIS with a Form I-212 waiver without reopening her proceedings.

Indeed, Ms. Delcarmen Lara may still be able to pursue adjustment of status before USCIS since she apparently is no longer in immigration proceedings. Practitioners should screen for this issue of execution of a removal order after leaving on advance parole when evaluating their clients’ eligibility for adjustment, as this may obviate the need to file a motion to reopen before the Executive Office for Immigration Review.

Prospective Application

The BIA determined that the new interpretation of departure under advance parole will be applied prospectively. It emphasized that Arrabally had been longstanding precedent, that the new rule represents a significant change, and that the government's interest in applying the new interpretation did not outweigh the reliance interests created by the former rule. This means that the decision does not apply to clients who traveled and returned on advance parole before Aug. 13, 2026.

The decision does not elaborate on what “prospective” means in every possible setting. For example, does it cover people who left on advance parole before Aug. 13, 2026, but returned on or after that date? Arguably yes, because they relied on the prior interpretation of the statute at the time they left. Practitioners may need to demonstrate their client’s reliance on Arrabally in those particular fact situations and argue that Delcarmen Lara does not apply to them.

What About Federal Appellate Court Decisions?

The Eleventh Circuit had previously applied Arrabally in Ortiz-Bouchet v. U.S. Attorney General, 714 F.3d 1353 (11th Cir. 2013). In that case, the appellate court followed the BIA decision and held that a departure under advance parole did not qualify as a departure under § 212(a)(9)(B). The BIA acknowledged this holding and stated that it did not read Ortiz-Bouchet as preventing it from revisiting its interpretation of “departure.” But practitioners practicing within that circuit can argue that Ortiz-Bouchet remains binding until the circuit itself rules otherwise.

More broadly, after the Supreme Court’s decision in Loper Bright Enterprises, 603 U.S. ___, 144 S. Ct. 2244 (2024), federal courts are no longer required to defer to an agency's interpretation or reinterpretation of a statutory term if the court determines it is ambiguous. Litigation over the new interpretation of “departure” and the precedential effect of Delcarmen-Lara seems highly likely.

What Practitioners Should Do Now

Immigration practitioners should consider taking the following steps:

Identify clients with outstanding advance parole documents. Advise them of the effects of departing now with that travel document if they have accrued more than 180 days of unlawful presence. Advise them of the effect of departing if they have an outstanding order of deportation or removal. Advise them that it is possible that they will be refused entry by CBP if they are determined to be inadmissible.

Hold off applying for advance parole for clients who are eligible but would be affected by the BIA decision. • Revise office forms, travel-consent language, and engagement letters. Advance parole counseling should expressly address § 212(a)(9)(B) and the Delcarmen-Lara decision.

Explain the consular processing path to permanent residency for clients who will no longer qualify for adjustment of status due to their having entered without inspection and their inability to depart under advance parole.

Develop more experience in filing I-601A provisional waivers for clients who will now have to consular process and trigger the unlawful presence bars upon their departure.

Watch for implementing guidance in a USCIS Policy Manual update or a follow-on BIA decision refining how "prospective" application will be measured.

Conclusion

The result in Delcarmen-Lara should not be surprising to practitioners who have watched the BIA issue dozens of precedential decisions over the past year and a half that nearly all favor the Trump administration’s extreme policies. The immediate impact of Delcarmen-Lara may be somewhat muted, as many noncitizens who traveled on advance parole did so prior to the effective date of the decision and thus can benefit from the more favorable Arrabally interpretation. And the lengthy processing time for Form I-131 advance parole applications — currently 23 months — has made applying for advance parole less desirable. But the long-term impact could be significant, making it far more difficult for noncitizens to obtain adjustment of status.

title: Amid Ongoing Conflict, Warner, Kaine, Colleagues Urge Trump Administration to Extend ...

The State Department maintains a Level 4: Do Not Travel advisory for the entire country, citing risks including armed conflict, civil unrest, and terrorism.

text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Sens. Mark R. Warner and Tim Kaine (both D-VA) led their colleagues in urging the Trump administration to extend and redesignate Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Sudan as ongoing violence and a worsening humanitarian crisis continue to put citizens at grave risk.

In a letter to Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the senators wrote, “After war erupted in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), DHS extended and redesignated Sudan for TPS, citing ongoing armed conflict, widespread violence, severe humanitarian conditions, mass displacement, and serious human rights abuses. DHS again extended Sudan’s TPS designation in 2025 after determining that these conditions continued to prevent the safe return of Sudanese nationals.”

TPS is a temporary, legal immigration status granted to foreign citizens in the U.S. who are endangered by conditions in their home country resulting from extraordinary events such as ongoing armed conflict, environmental disaster, or epidemic. TPS status is granted for set periods ranging from six to 18 months, requiring the Department of Homeland Security to extend a country’s status on a recurring basis. Each time a country is recertified, recipients must reapply and pass a thorough background check. Sudan’s current TPS designation is set to expire October 19, 2026. An extension and redesignation would protect current Sudanese TPS holders from returning to the country amid its ongoing conflict and would offer protected status to Sudanese nationals who arrived in the United States after August 16, 2023.

The senators highlighted the mounting crisis in Sudan, adding, “The armed conflict between the SAF and the RSF has intensified and expanded, causing one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. Fighting has spread across much of the country, resulting in tens of thousands of deaths, the displacement of millions of people, widespread destruction of civilian infrastructure, severe food insecurity, and credible reports of war crimes and other serious human rights violations. The U.S. government has determined that the RSF and SAF have committed war crimes and that the RSF is responsible for crimes against humanity and genocide. Secretary Rubio has further recognized the genocide in Sudan and joined G7 countries in warning against further atrocities in El Obeid in July 2026.”

“Humanitarian access remains severely restricted, and large areas of Sudan continue to be unsafe for civilians, making the return of Sudanese nationals unsafe under current conditions. Sudan continues to face catastrophic humanitarian conditions – including the risk of famine in several areas – that have been compounded by climate shocks, widespread food insecurity, and the destruction of critical infrastructure. Since the outbreak of the war in April 2023, hospitals, schools, water systems, roads, and electrical infrastructure have been damaged or destroyed, severely limiting access to basic services and humanitarian assistance,” the senators continued.

The senators also noted that the Trump administration has already acknowledged the dangers posed by the war and humanitarian crisis in Sudan. The State Department maintains a Level 4: Do Not Travel advisory for the entire country, citing risks including armed conflict, civil unrest, and terrorism. Furthermore, the U.S. Embassy in Khartoum has suspended operations since April 2023, leaving the U.S. government unable to provide routine or emergency consular services to U.S. citizens in Sudan.

In addition to Sens. Warner and Kaine, the letter was signed by Sens. Michael Bennet (D-CO), Adam Schiff (D-CA), Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), Tammy Duckworth (D-IL), Cory Booker (D-NJ), and Raphael Warnock (D-GA).

Since the conflict erupted, Sens. Warner and Kaine have been outspoken voices in the Senate on the need for increased diplomatic and humanitarian support for Sudan. In June 2025, the senators sponsored the Safe Environment from Countries Under Repression and Emergency (SECURE) Act, legislation to provide qualified TPS and Deferred Enforced Departure (DED) recipients a path to legal permanent residency. In January 2025, Sens. Warner and Kaine urged then-President Biden to extend or redesignate TPS for all 17 TPS-eligible countries, including Sudan. The senators have fought to strengthen the U.S. response to the Sudan crisis, introducing the Response to Conflict in Sudan Act to bolster and coordinate the U.S. response to the war in Sudan by codifying the Special Envoy for Sudan position at the U.S. Department of State. In December 2024, Sen. Warner urged the Biden administration to take more decisive action against foreign entities fueling the ongoing civil war in Sudan. In May 2023, Sens. Warner and Kaine led a group of colleagues in urging the administration to offer all available support for humanitarian efforts in the region – and to be forward-leaning on prioritizing local and community-based response efforts – as well as appoint a Special Envoy to Sudan tasked with coordinating and leading U.S. diplomatic efforts to address the crisis. That same year, the senators also successfully called on the Biden administration to redesignate TPS for Sudan.

Read the full letter here and below.

Dear Secretary Mullin and Secretary Rubio:

We write to urge you to issue an 18-month extension and redesignation of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Sudan. The ongoing violence and humanitarian crisis in Sudan continue to place its citizens at severe risk. An extension would protect current Sudanese TPS holders from returning to Sudan amid ongoing violence, and a redesignation would offer protected status to Sudanese nationals who arrived after August 16, 2023.

After war erupted in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), DHS extended and redesignated Sudan for TPS, citing ongoing armed conflict, widespread violence, severe humanitarian conditions, mass displacement, and serious human rights abuses. DHS again extended Sudan’s TPS designation in 2025 after determining that these conditions continued to prevent the safe return of Sudanese nationals.

The armed conflict between the SAF and the RSF has intensified and expanded, causing one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. Fighting has spread across much of the country, resulting in tens of thousands of deaths, the displacement of millions of people, widespread destruction of civilian infrastructure, severe food insecurity, and credible reports of war crimes and other serious human rights violations. The U.S. government has determined that the RSF and SAF have committed war crimes and that the RSF is responsible for crimes against humanity and genocide. Secretary Rubio has further recognized the genocide in Sudan and joined G7 countries in warning against further atrocities in El Obeid in July 2026.

Humanitarian access remains severely restricted, and large areas of Sudan continue to be unsafe for civilians, making the return of Sudanese nationals unsafe under current conditions. Sudan continues to face catastrophic humanitarian conditions – including the risk of famine in several areas – that have been compounded by climate shocks, widespread food insecurity, and the destruction of critical infrastructure. Since the outbreak of the war in April 2023, hospitals, schools, water systems, roads, and electrical infrastructure have been damaged or destroyed, severely limiting access to basic services and humanitarian assistance.

More than 30 million people – two-thirds of Sudan’s population – are in need of humanitarian assistance, including 15 million children. More than 8 million people are internally displaced, making Sudan the world’s largest internal displacement crisis. Millions more have fled to neighboring countries as refugees. Humanitarian organizations continue to warn that funding shortfalls, ongoing insecurity, and restrictions on aid delivery are preventing life-saving assistance from reaching millions of people in need. These overlapping crises – ongoing armed conflict, mass displacement, widespread hunger, disease outbreaks, climate-related disasters, and the collapse of essential services – have significantly worsened since Sudan’s most recent TPS designation and continue to make the safe return of Sudanese nationals impossible.

The posture of the State Department demonstrates the dangers of the war in Sudan. The U.S. Department of State currently maintains a Level 4: Do Not Travel advisory for all of Sudan, warning U.S. citizens not to travel to the country due to ongoing armed conflict, civil unrest, crime, kidnapping, terrorism, landmines, and serious health and security risks. The State Department also notes that the U.S. Embassy in Khartoum has suspended operations since April 2023 and that the U.S. government cannot provide routine or emergency consular services to U.S. citizens in Sudan. These conditions underscore the continued instability throughout the country and further demonstrate that Sudan remains unsafe for the return of Sudanese nationals.

At the beginning of this administration, approximately 1.2 million foreign nationals were protected under TPS, including 1,790 individuals from Sudan. These individuals make significant contributions to the U.S. economy and the communities they call home. They are taxpayers, consumers, entrepreneurs, and essential members of the workforce. According to the American Immigration Council, TPS holders collectively generated more than $10.3 billion in household income, held nearly $8 billion in spending power, and contributed over $2.2 billion in federal, state, and local taxes in 2021 alone. Beyond these measurable economic contributions, TPS holders strengthen local economies by purchasing homes, renting apartments, starting businesses, and filling critical labor shortages across a range of industries. Although Sudanese TPS beneficiaries represent only a portion of the overall TPS population, they likewise contribute to the U.S. workforce and economy while lawfully employed under TPS.

In light of these circumstances, we strongly urge you to extend and redesignate Sudan for TPS. The ongoing armed conflict, catastrophic humanitarian crisis, and widespread human rights abuses make the safe return of Sudanese nationals impossible at this time, meeting the legal standard for extension and redesignation of TPS under Sec. 244 of the Immigration and Nationality Act. text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is pitching a plan to help shield local police officers who make immigration arrests from possible financial consequences if they are accused of on-duty misconduct.

The agency is proposing to subsidize liability insurance for state and local officers who are trained and deputized to enforce federal immigration laws, according to a planning document published Friday.

ICE’s partnerships with local departments have soared since President Donald Trump returned to the White House last year and may get an additional boost with liability insurance by removing a hurdle that has made some local police departments reluctant to join. The Associated Press is the first to report on this insurance proposal.

Under the plan, officers would purchase insurance covering up to $500,000 in personal liability, which typically funds legal fees, settlements and judgments. Officers would be reimbursed up to $250 annually — roughly what the insurance is expected to cost.

One prominent critic of ICE’s immigration crackdown said the program would be yet another way for officers to avoid personal accountability for misconduct.

“The concern here is that ICE is going above and beyond to guarantee law enforcement does not have even the slightest risk of liability for violating Americans’ rights while helping ICE arrest people,” said David Bier, director of immigration studies at the Cato Institute, who has called on Congress to make it easier to sue ICE agents for wrongdoing.

ICE outlined the plan in a document informing industry officials that it is considering hiring a contractor to help provide outreach, training and communications support for its so-called 287(g) partnerships with local departments, which are named for a section of a 1996 immigration law. The contractor would hire the insurance vendor and process the reimbursements, among other tasks.

ICE has asked for industry feedback by Thursday. The proposed timeline for launching the program and its estimated cost are unclear.

ICE had no immediate comment on the plan.

Arrests by ICE’s local partners have spiked since last year

During Trump’s second term, ICE has offered generous financial incentives to participating local agencies, increasing the number who have partnered with the federal government, as well as the number of arrests.

Nearly 1,600 agencies in 32 states now have agreements to participate in ICE’s task force model, in which trained local officers can interrogate, arrest and charge people suspected of being in the country illegally, according to ICE data.

Departments qualify for funding to help cover expenses like their officers’ pay, equipment and vehicles. With encouragement from state and local Republican officials, agencies in Florida, Texas, Oklahoma and Georgia have been among the leaders.

Arrests made through such programs jumped to an average of 3,000 per month in the first two months of 2026, according to the most recent ICE data provided to the University of California Berkeley’s Deportation Data Project. That compares to a monthly average of 250 in 2024 under President Joe Biden.

Local departments, officers worried about liability for ICE work

As local officers increasingly carry out federal immigration work, they and their departments have expressed concerns about the civil liability that could result from claims alleging excessive use of force, wrongful arrest and illegal search and seizure, among other things.

That’s because insurance policies that cover their local work may not apply. Pennsylvania’s risk pool, for instance, recently made clear that it would exclude “proactive immigration enforcement activities” from coverage, forcing several participating counties to search for other insurance options.

Butler County Sheriff Michael Slupe said he found insurance to cover his 13 deputies participating in the program at a cost of $20,000 in annual premiums.

“I want to make sure the guys are additionally covered, so we had to spend the money,” he said, adding that federal funding would cover the cost.

Federal officers usually enjoy legal immunities and a government-funded defense when they face lawsuits. But those protections may not always apply to local officers, which has heightened their concerns over liability and the need for insurance.

While civil lawsuits are the main concern, professional liability insurance typically helps cover legal fees for officers facing criminal investigations as well.

Sheriffs’ group says ICE’s insurance idea sounds promising

Justin Smith, a former Colorado sheriff who is executive director of the National Sheriffs’ Association, said ICE’s plan sounds promising and that he was anxious to speak with ICE about how the plan would work.

Smith said he has shared concerns with ICE that some sheriffs are reluctant to join the partnerships because of the potential liability at a time when immigration enforcement faces intense public protests and media scrutiny. Smith said others who are partnering with ICE have already started facing legal claims tied to their immigration work, which can be costly whether or not deputies are ultimately found to have done anything wrong.

“Right now, any time you are working on immigration there is going to be a much higher potential for there being problems and having suits and issues,” he said. “They’re recognizing that it is a different environment. And I think trying to be good partners with us as best they can.”

Under their agreements, ICE warns local departments that they are responsible for the costs of incidents that give rise to liability. But it seeks to reduce the risk by saying local officers performing ICE-authorized functions are “acting under color of federal authority,” which would bar lawsuits against individual officers.

The agreements also state that local officers who face civil lawsuits can ask the U.S. Department of Justice to represent them, and that ICE will generally support their requests. But the final decision on whether to do so rests with DOJ.

text:
McCOOK — The sun was still rising as nearly 60 “mothers and others” boarded an Omaha bus and headed across the state to protest what goes on at the ICE detention facility in rural McCook.

Their nearly 10-hour round trip marked a year since Gov. Jim Pillen announced the deal he made with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to convert the state’s rehabilitative-focused Work Ethic Camp into a 300-bed jail for migrants. The bus passengers, set to join other like-minded rallygoers Saturday, wanted McCook, the state and nation to know that time had not dulled their contempt for that decision or concern for those detained.

They carried signs: “We have not forgotten.”

Despite attempts by some state lawmakers and a lawsuit by 13 McCook residents to halt the plan, the ICE jail began accepting foreign-born detainees in November and the daily population count through March fluctuated between about 100 and 171, according to the Deportation Data Project, a repository of immigration enforcement data maintained by the University of California Berkeley Law School and obtained through the Freedom of Information Act.

Pillen last year said he expected the feds would pay the state a $2.45 million “base” fee each month. But to date, the state has received $14.6 million: $9.3 million based on occupied beds and $5.3 million for one-time costs such as vehicles and equipment, said a spokesperson for the Nebraska Department of Correctional Services.

Spokesperson Dayne Urbanovsky, in an email to the Examiner, said the higher amount could come when the facility is able to house 300. She said renovations are to be completed later this summer.

Responding to the rally, Pillen spokesperson Laura Strimple said the governor remains committed to the ICE partnership and to “safe and secure detention of illegal detainees accused of either criminal or civil violations of our nation’s laws.”

The “McCook detention center has served that purpose for ICE and the Department of Homeland Security and will continue to do so throughout its contract with the state,” Strimple said. The contract is valid through at least September 2027.

As the Omaha bus pulled up to the rally site, a private lot within eyeshot of the detention facility, passengers held up letters that spelled “Omaha Cares.” The bus was hosted by “Mothers and Others: Justice and Mercy for Immigrants,” but carried representatives of assorted organizations, including a Nebraska lawmaker.

They joined a rally that grew to about 300 people. Lead organizers — including McCook-based Nebraska Voices, Lincoln-based Taco Tuesday Familia and American Civil Liberties Union Nebraska — said the turnout, higher than previous protests, signaled a continued resolve to fight for due process and legal reform for migrants.

Organizers said participation, spanning the state, reflected a growing network of advocacy entities watching actions of ICE and the McCook facility.

“It’s galvanized people’s sense of injustice,” said Nebraska Voices’ Lorri Sughroue, who helped form the McCook group last year.

‘This began in 1492’

Kevin Abourezk, a Lakota elder whose journalism career documented stories of indigenous people, kicked off the rally’s lineup of speakers, saying the only people who aren’t immigrants are Native Americans.

Abourezk touched upon U.S. history and said the reason for Saturday’s gathering did not begin just last year. “This began in 1492, when Columbus landed …”

He told demonstrators that perhaps it is “good and right to have standards by which people are allowed to come here” to carve out homes for their families. He pointed toward the nearby McCook detention center: “But in terms of smart immigration reform — it ain’t that.”

The two-hour program that unfolded without incident also included musicians, bilingual poets, red-robed Handmaids of Nebraska, hatted “Pissed Off Grandmas,” words from Las Voces Nebraska, clergy and local McCook residents.

Most wore shirts with immigrant-friendly messages. Dozens held signs and waved to passing motorists on U.S. Highway 83 in the Red Willow County town of about 7,500.

Co-organizer Holly Burns spoke of her Latino family’s Nebraska roots, which started with her grandparents’ farm work in Scotts Bluff County and led to Lincoln where she and sister Tiffany last year formed the Taco Tuesday Familia advocacy group.

She spoke of how certain U.S. states were once part of Mexico. “Truly in my family’s history, the border crossed us,” said Burns.

State Sen. Margo Juarez of South Omaha got one of the louder reactions when recounting a meeting she and another lawmaker had the prior week with state officials about “isolation rooms” under construction at the McCook facility. She said she has asked for an accounting of how they are used.

Mindy Rush Chipman, executive director of ACLU Nebraska, harked back to Pillen’s August 2025 announcement that the state would convert the Work Ethic Camp into an ICE jail.

“Those plans were shrouded in secrecy,” she told those sitting in lawn chairs, on the ground and under tents.

Out of 49 lawmakers in an officially nonpartisan Nebraska Legislature, a group of 13 Democrats and one independent demanded more transparency and questioned whether Pillen violated the Nebraska Constitution by repurposing the state correctional facility without direct legislative approval. Pillen has argued that he is doing his duty to help the federal government enforce immigration laws.

A Red Willow County district judge ruled in favor of the governor and later dismissed a lawsuit filed by Nebraska Appleseed on behalf of a group of McCook residents and former State Sen. DiAnna Schimek. The judge said that the Legislature had previously tasked the executive branch with managing state prisons, and that the Pillen administration legally entered into the ICE contract. Appleseed has appealed the decision.

Rush Chipman also told rallygoers that most ICE detainees are not dangerous or criminals, though held for civil violations of being in the country without authorization. The Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse at Syracuse University (TRAC), a nonprofit that tracks immigration trends, showed about 70% of migrants in ICE detention have no criminal convictions.

“They’re people that are being taken away from their families, taken away from their jobs and taken away from the communities they call home,” Rush Chipman said.

ACLU attorney Grant Friedman said that in his experiences, the McCook detention center provides the “worst lawyer-client accommodations.” He said, for example, he can’t get a message to an inmate without a full name and immigration identification number, which he said detainees don’t always have.

At the same time Pillen announced the facility, he disclosed a new 287(g) pact between ICE and the Nebraska State Patrol — a move Rush Chipman said essentially turned the state agency into an extension of immigration enforcement.

Initially, six troopers were trained as 287(g) task force officers. A patrol spokesman confirmed that the number has grown to 16.

Spokesman Cody Thomas said that since August, state troopers have assisted in about 275 immigration-related detentions or transports in 30 Nebraska counties, and that Homeland Security has reimbursed the patrol $277,037.

A few recent encounters he cited included a case when a trooper detained an undocumented migrant with several prior convictions including disorderly conduct and DUI, and another in which the person had a prior child sexual assault.

Thomas said the near tripling of troopers trained for immigration duties was due to unpredictable scheduling demands and new state participation in a program to “locate and ensure the safety of unaccompanied children.”

No detentions have resulted in the program to find unaccompanied children, he said, but the task force helped find over 10 youths “and ensured they were safely with family.”

Nationally, 287(g) partnerships have increased from 135 to 2,179 since the beginning of President Trump’s second term, a Homeland Security spokesperson said.

Solidarity appreciated

For some residents of McCook, a High Plains town historically tied to railroads and agriculture, the weekend gathering was a welcome sign of solidarity.

Sughroue said many locals are fervent in their support for toughened ICE enforcement, though she also believes a good chunk don’t want the detention facility in their backyard. She believes they’re silenced by potential “repercussions” in the largely conservative area.

Indeed, a few asked not to be identified in a story.

John and Deborah Walters are registered Republicans who said they won’t hold back their objections.

The couple owns ag land in the area, including the few acres on which the rally was held. They said they learned about the plan for the McCook ICE facility on a national newscast while eating breakfast at a hotel in Iowa.

“We were shocked,” said John, born in McCook 79 years ago. He believes state officials did not weigh future effects on the area. Deborah described as “our neighbors” most of the immigrants arrested in President Donald Trump’s mass deportation movement. Both were disturbed when federal and state officials dubbed the facility the “Cornhusker Clink.”

“Everything’s been so secretive, that’s what bothers us,” Deborah said. “It’s a perfect location, right? Rural Nebraska, nobody is going to complain.”

The couple viewed Saturday’s turnout as “tremendous.”

Gary Power, 84, said he endured the afternoon heat to register support “for democracy” and against inhumane tactics. He said he was somewhat surprised to see so many McCook folks.

“Six months ago I would never have seen something like this,” said Power. “They woke up. They’re paying those gas prices, wouldn’t that wake you up?”

McCook resident Diane Lyons told the group that part of her anxiety is not knowing what will come later of the converted facility now surrounded with new “rows and rows and rows of barbed wire.” She said she valued its previous use as a work ethic camp whose inmates helped set up various community events, including Santa Claus Lane.

“We feel your fear,” she told the group. “We feel the anxiety. We feel the anger about the people that are being wrongfully detained there … we also have lost a lot.”

Helping hands

Looking back over the past year, advocates said they are encouraged to see a stronger network emerge to help respond to immigration-related needs.

The connections played out in a recent situation when a former McCook detainee from Minnesota called a North Platte advocacy group about his friend newly released from the McCook facility. The friend, a Spanish-speaking Venezuelan, wound up in Omaha without a phone, food or resources. The North Platte advocate called a representative of Omaha Welcomes the Stranger nonprofit, who contacted a member of Mothers and Others, who found the former detainee (via help of a photo) sitting alone in a lot near the Omaha immigration court complex. Volunteers at Omaha Welcomes the Stranger provided the Venezuelan a place to stay and helped him return to his family and friends in Minnesota.

Looking ahead, rallygoers in McCook are seeking to build a fellowship program that interacts with detainees. Appleseed continues its legal quest to close the facility.

“Working together helps protect our communities and encourages others around us to demand better from our elected officials,” Rush Chipman told the rally. “If Florida can close its detention center, so can we.”

As the Omaha bus returned about 8 p.m., riders were signing up for another protest at a Council Bluffs ICE detention facility.

Juarez was planning another visit with McCook detainees. She had asked to do so the day of the rally, but was told more notice was needed.

“We need to continue to monitor what goes on at the facility especially now that they have those isolation rooms,” she said.

The South Omaha lawmaker, a member of Mothers for Others, said she will work to end the McCook ICE partnership when the current contract ends in fall 2027. She said she left the rally energized by the geographic representation, diversity and number of young participants.

“There were so many young people there who saw the wrong in the facility — that’s inspiring to me,” she said. “I hope they continue with their concern and leadership and always speak out on issues they don’t feel are humane.”

Chellie Pingree told an audience of about 200 people who gathered in a high school gym on Monday.

She said the intended target was Durán Guerrero’s roommate, and that he did not have a final order of removal from the U.S., despite an Immigration and Customs Enforcement statement shortly after the shooting that said it was targeting someone with such an order.

Pingree called it a “shocking revelation,” that “clearly contradicts” what ICE and the Department of Homeland Security have been saying.

But later, talking to reporters in the school’s gym, Pingree said the information she shared came from reporting in the Washington Post (though the Post has not actually reported the roommate was the target). “It has not been confirmed to us by ICE,” Pingree clarified.

The confusion over the person she then referred to as the “presumed target” was a revealing demonstration of just how much congressional Democrats have been left in the dark by the Trump administration.

The killing of Durán Guerrero, 25, has caused protests in several Maine cities. Residents want to know the circumstances of his death, but so far ICE and DHS have not explained what happened and have not said anything about the identity of the shooter or his vetting and training for the job.

On Monday, two members of the House Homeland Security Committee, as well as the second-most senior Democrat in the House, joined Pingree in Biddeford for what they dubbed a “shadow hearing” to conduct oversight of ICE and DHS. They said it was necessary because the Republican chair of the Homeland Security Committee hasn’t called an official oversight hearing since February.

They repeatedly said that whatever information they had came from media reports.

Despite their frustration and interest in holding ICE accountable for acts of violence in several U.S. communities, the Democrats who put on the event in Biddeford said they had not gotten answers to any of their myriad questions about ICE’s practices, and they had no information about to what extent the FBI or DHS Inspector General are investigating Durán Guerrero’s death.

Still, the hearing was a chance for top Democrats to hear directly from the southern Maine community, immigrant advocates and Durán Guerrero’s family about their concerns and what they want Congress to do.

Rep. Bennie Thompson of Mississippi, the senior Democrat on the House Homeland Security Committee, said he cried before the hearing with Durán Guerrero’s parents, Dora Guerrero and Omar Durán Plata, who live in Colombia and were present at the event.

The family’s attorney, Ben Gideon, said it took courage for them to come to the United States from Colombia after their son was killed by a federal agent.

Victim’s parents attend hearing

Durán Plata spoke briefly to the four members of Congress on stage and the roughly 200 people in the crowd. He described his son as honest, responsible and loving, and said “we do not know how to go on with life without you.” He said Durán Guerrero’s 3-year-old daughter, Dulce, asks why her father doesn’t come home from work.

“I ask of God and the justice system that my son’s case be brought to light,” he said.

Biddeford Mayor Liam LaFountain said the city has not heard from anyone at ICE or DHS. Gideon said Durán Guerrero’s family members have not heard from those agencies, either, and he asserted that the FBI and DHS Inspector General are not actively investigating.

“We’ve had our own investigative team out on the ground, and they have not encountered any federal investigation going on anywhere in Maine,” Gideon told reporters after the hearing.

Several audience members said in interviews that they’re skeptical about whether there will be accountability for the shooting.

The office of Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey is leading a state investigation, though his office did not participate in Monday’s hearing. In a statement released afterward, Frey said his office “continues to actively investigate the shooting.”

“This office has been collecting, processing, and analyzing evidence to determine whether Maine law authorizes legal action to address the conduct,” the statement said.

Gov. Janet Mills spoke briefly, saying she has “full confidence” in Frey’s office, “that they’ll complete a thorough investigation into the facts of this tragedy, and they’ll report them to the public in due course.”

The governor, a former prosecutor, got emotional talking about the U.S. Constitution and how she believes ICE is endangering people in Maine.

“This has to end, and if ICE cannot be fundamentally reformed, then it is time to abolish it,” she said. The crowd cheered. Throughout the hearing scattered voices in the audience shouted out, “We do not feel safe,” or “Abolish ICE,” or “Close it down.”

Members of Congress and the witnesses they called to speak at the hearing argued Durán Guerrero’s killing was an intentional outcome of Trump administration policy. In addition to Pingree and Thompson, it included Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts and Rep. Troy Carter of New Orleans. Thompson said he invited Republicans on the Homeland Security Committee but they did not attend.

“ICE is a danger to every community in which they are active if they are not held accountable,” Clark said. She called the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement “state-sanctioned terror.”

Shortly after the Biddeford shooting, President Donald Trump said on social media, “The men and women of ICE are doing a GREAT job, one that has to be done.”

On his way to work

Durán Guerrero had gotten in a car to go to work the morning of the shooting. Gideon said Monday that there were five gunshots. Pingree questioned whether the ICE agent knew whom he was shooting at.

This month, local artists created a 15-foot mural of Durán Guerrero and his daughter on the side of a building near the corner of Main and Alfred streets.

Durán Guerrero’s family allowed state investigators to take and search the car, though they told the Portland Press Herald they want his legal documents back, which will help them repatriate Durán Guerrero’s remains to Colombia so he can be buried there.

In the audience Monday, Dick Bennett, of Biddeford, said he wants to know what has happened to the ICE agent who shot Durán Guerrero. He’s been identified by an ex-wife as David Brouillette, though Brouillette hasn’t responded to requests for an interview and a phone number for him is not in service.

“I believe nothing will happen to him and I don’t have faith he’ll be prosecuted,” Bennett said.

Katherine Rielly, of Buxton, said she didn’t understand why the attorney general’s office hasn’t taken any public steps toward a prosecution.

“If it was anyone else they would’ve arrested the person already,” she said. She worries the state will defer to federal authorities.

In response to concerns like those, the attorney general’s office said in its statement, “protecting the integrity of the investigation takes priority while evidence is still being gathered.”

Pingree told reporters that she doesn’t know anything about where Brouillette is or whether he still works for ICE.

Some of the biggest applause at the hearing was for LaFountain, who said his city and others have born a burden for aggressive immigration enforcement.

“A federal force came into my city, exercised one of the most extraordinary powers that governments possess — the use of deadly force — and left the consequences for Johan’s family and our city to carry,” he said.

“Immigrant residents in my city, including people with legal status, are afraid to go about their daily lives.”

Thompson said on July 15, every Democratic member of Congress signed a letter asking for details about the killing in Biddeford. To this day, he said, they have not received a reply from DHS or ICE.

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is pitching a plan to help shield local police officers who make immigration arrests from possible financial consequences if they are accused of on-duty misconduct.

The agency is proposing to subsidize liability insurance for state and local officers who are trained and deputized to enforce federal immigration laws, according to a planning document published Friday.

ICE’s partnerships with local departments have soared since President Donald Trump returned to the White House last year and may get an additional boost with liability insurance by removing a hurdle that has made some local police departments reluctant to join. The Associated Press is the first to report on this insurance proposal.

Under the plan, officers would purchase insurance covering up to $500,000 in personal liability, which typically funds legal fees, settlements and judgments. Officers would be reimbursed up to $250 annually — roughly what the insurance is expected to cost.

One prominent critic of ICE’s immigration crackdown said the program would be yet another way for officers to avoid personal accountability for misconduct.

“The concern here is that ICE is going above and beyond to guarantee law enforcement does not have even the slightest risk of liability for violating Americans’ rights while helping ICE arrest people,” said David Bier, director of immigration studies at the Cato Institute, who has called on Congress to make it easier to sue ICE agents for wrongdoing.

ICE outlined the plan in a document informing industry officials that it is considering hiring a contractor to help provide outreach, training and communications support for its so-called 287(g) partnerships with local departments, which are named for a section of a 1996 immigration law. The contractor would hire the insurance vendor and process the reimbursements, among other tasks.

ICE has asked for industry feedback by Thursday. The proposed timeline for launching the program and its estimated cost are unclear.

ICE had no immediate comment on the plan.

Arrests by ICE’s local partners have spiked since last year

During Trump’s second term, ICE has offered generous financial incentives to participating local agencies, increasing the number who have partnered with the federal government, as well as the number of arrests.

Nearly 1,600 agencies in 32 states now have agreements to participate in ICE’s task force model, in which trained local officers can interrogate, arrest and charge people suspected of being in the country illegally, according to ICE data.

Departments qualify for funding to help cover expenses like their officers’ pay, equipment and vehicles. With encouragement from state and local Republican officials, agencies in Florida, Texas, Oklahoma and Georgia have been among the leaders.

Arrests made through such programs jumped to an average of 3,000 per month in the first two months of 2026, according to the most recent ICE data provided to the University of California Berkeley’s Deportation Data Project. That compares to a monthly average of 250 in 2024 under President Joe Biden.

Local departments, officers worried about liability for ICE work

As local officers increasingly carry out federal immigration work, they and their departments have expressed concerns about the civil liability that could result from claims alleging excessive use of force, wrongful arrest and illegal search and seizure, among other things.

That’s because insurance policies that cover their local work may not apply. Pennsylvania’s risk pool, for instance, recently made clear that it would exclude “proactive immigration enforcement activities” from coverage, forcing several participating counties to search for other insurance options.

Butler County Sheriff Michael Slupe said he found insurance to cover his 13 deputies participating in the program at a cost of $20,000 in annual premiums.

“I want to make sure the guys are additionally covered, so we had to spend the money,” he said, adding that federal funding would cover the cost.

Federal officers usually enjoy legal immunities and a government-funded defense when they face lawsuits. But those protections may not always apply to local officers, which has heightened their concerns over liability and the need for insurance.

While civil lawsuits are the main concern, professional liability insurance typically helps cover legal fees for officers facing criminal investigations as well.

Sheriffs’ group says ICE’s insurance idea sounds promising

Justin Smith, a former Colorado sheriff who is executive director of the National Sheriffs’ Association, said ICE’s plan sounds promising and that he was anxious to speak with ICE about how the plan would work.

Smith said he has shared concerns with ICE that some sheriffs are reluctant to join the partnerships because of the potential liability at a time when immigration enforcement faces intense public protests and media scrutiny. Smith said others who are partnering with ICE have already started facing legal claims tied to their immigration work, which can be costly whether or not deputies are ultimately found to have done anything wrong.

“Right now, any time you are working on immigration there is going to be a much higher potential for there being problems and having suits and issues,” he said. “They’re recognizing that it is a different environment. And I think trying to be good partners with us as best they can.”

Under their agreements, ICE warns local departments that they are responsible for the costs of incidents that give rise to liability. But it seeks to reduce the risk by saying local officers performing ICE-authorized functions are “acting under color of federal authority,” which would bar lawsuits against individual officers.

The agreements also state that local officers who face civil lawsuits can ask the U.S. Department of Justice to represent them, and that ICE will generally support their requests. But the final decision on whether to do so rests with DOJ.

Representative Bennie Thompson, ranking Democrat on the House Homeland Security committee, vowed to conduct an official investigation into the shooting if Democrats retake majority control in November.

Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey meanwhile said his office continues to investigate the shooting.

Maine law says the AG's office is responsible for investigating deadly use of force by law enforcement and presenting findings to the Maine Deadly Force Review Panel.

In a statement on Monday, Frey said the panel can then make recommendations but does not have jurisdiction over the Department of Homeland Security.

He said the Trump administration or Congress will be responsible for answering any questions that arise from the review.

Customs and Border Protection is pausing construction in Big Bend National Park, CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott said in an X post on Monday.

Scott's announcement comes amid several lawsuits that have been filed to stop border wall-related construction in the Texas national park. CBP was building parts of a "limited" barrier in the park instead of a 30-foot-wall as initially intended.

"CBP is pausing all construction activity in Big Bend National Park while I visit and conduct a personal, on-the-ground evaluation," Scott said. "CBP is firmly committed to protecting America, and that includes our national treasures like Big Bend National Park (BBNP). We know the current and predictable national security threats, and they are real."

Texas Sen. John Cornyn, a Republican, wrote a letter to Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin about the construction in early August.

"Recently, a bipartisan group of Texas border sheriffs and county judges, private landowners, and the Big Bend Park advocates have raised significant concerns about DHS' proposed construction of border barriers in Big Bend National Park and Big Bend Ranch State Park," Cornyn wrote.

He noted that many residents live and work around the park are concerned a wall would ruin the landscape, threaten native American sites and disrupt wildlife migration and harm the local economy.

Former Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem waived certain laws which allowed the construction to get underway.

Last week, Texas State Sen. Roland Gutierrez, a Democrat, joined ABC News Live's Kyra Phillips for his first TV interview about his federal lawsuit against the Trump administration over proposed border barriers in Big Bend National Park.

Gutierrez said last week that the project threatens sacred land, archaeological sites and national resources, and claimed crews have already clear-cut roughly two miles of land.

He questioned the need for barriers in the remote area, called the project a waste of taxpayer money and argued that the administration must follow laws protecting national parkland.

Join the Schell Center for International Human Rights and Migration that Works(link is external)5 for a timely panel discussion centered on how expansion of the temporary visa (or guestworker) programs could impact workers in the state of Connecticut and beyond. The panel will cover the current state of the guestworker programs, with key information about our current immigration context and the guestworker programs’ impacts on workers and families; and timely opportunities to protect Connecticut workers and advance an alternative human rights based model for labor migration.

Over a million people have lost or stand to lose their temporary protected status (TPS), including work permits and protection from deportation, after the Supreme Court’s recent decision allowing the administration to end TPS for Haiti and Syria and endangering TPS for people from many other countries. Countless immigrant families and people seeking asylum are being stripped of their work permits and targeted for detention and deportation. Families fear the devastating consequences of these policies. As many as 9,460 people with TPS and 682,000 immigrants in Connecticut could be impacted by these policies. And many Connecticut communities and employers worry about the economy and labor shortages that will ensue or be exacerbated.

Instead of protecting our immigrant and migrant communities, proposals in Congress would expand the guestworker programs to fill labor shortages. These programs are fundamentally flawed: they tie migrant workers to their employers, dissuading workers from speaking up when they face wage theft, unsafe working conditions, or discrimination, making them vulnerable to retaliation, forced labor, and other human rights abuses. By lowering the floor for worker protections, expanding these programs will harm workers’ wages and working conditions. These developments raise fundamental questions of international human rights law — including non-refoulement, freedom from forced labor, and the rights of migrant workers — that are increasingly playing out in Connecticut's own communities and economy.
