title: The buck stops elsewhere: When things go awry, Trump deflects blame - LA Times
description:
It is among the most famous phrases in presidential history: “The buck stops here.” Except with President Trump, it almost never does.
The White House counters that Trump is working to correct long-festering challenges, not simply throwing up his hands and ignoring them.
A pattern dating to Trump’s first term Truman famously kept a “the buck stops here” sign on his desk as president.
“The buck stops with everybody,” Trump said in 2019, during a lengthy government shutdown.
“The buck stops here with me,” he said then.
text:
It is among the most famous phrases in presidential history: “The buck stops here.” Except with President Trump, it almost never does.

Concerns about a weak economy and still-high inflation? His predecessor, President Biden, saddled him with that, he says, even though the Democrat has been out of office for 18-plus months and despite Trump once promising an immediate turnaround.

The problem-plagued revamp of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool? That was marred by vandalism, the president insists, even though the office of a prosecutor he put in the job has said the damage was due to shoddy workmanship.

The increasingly unpopular war in Iran that has kept oil prices high, Trump’s approval rating low and sent shock waves through the global economy? Actually, this was Trump making up for timid earlier presidents who, he argues, squandered nearly 50 years of opportunities to curb Iran’s nuclear ambitions.

Pithy slogans aside, all modern presidents shift responsibility onto others to some degree, frequently blaming the White House occupant who preceded them or Congress — or both. But Trump has taken it to a new level, essentially embracing a de facto political strategy of being in charge of everything but responsible for nothing when things go badly.

“Taking responsibility being a characteristic of presidential leadership — or any kind of leadership — is absolutely true,” said Nicole Anslover, a history professor at Florida Atlantic University and author of “Harry S. Truman: The Coming of the Cold War.”

Trump’s tendency to point fingers at others is increasingly in the spotlight in the run-up to November’s midterm elections, when Republicans are trying to retain control of Congress. His unwillingness to accept blame sometimes leads him to deny that there are problems at all, and could leave GOP leaders in tight races with little reassurance for voters that their concerns are being addressed.

The White House counters that Trump is working to correct long-festering challenges, not simply throwing up his hands and ignoring them.

The president is “rightfully addressing the failures of his predecessors while taking action to deliver big wins for the American people,” spokesperson Taylor Rogers said, pointing to a series of policies that she said Republicans can run on, including tax cuts, efforts to lower prescription drug prices, cracking down on immigration and the U.S.-Mexico border, increasing domestic energy production and a strong stock market.

A pattern dating to Trump’s first term

Truman famously kept a “the buck stops here” sign on his desk as president. That came from “pass the buck,” which, according to Truman’s presidential library, dates to frontier times, when poker players would pass a buckhorn handle knife to the person whose turn it was to deal the cards.

“The president, whoever he is, has to decide,” Truman said during his farewell address in 1953. “He can’t pass the buck to anybody. No one else can do the deciding for him. That’s his job.”

The understanding of the phrase has broadened over the years to include taking responsibility for the outcome of tough decisions. Trump used to espouse similar beliefs, saying back in 2013 that in running a business, “Whatever happens, you’re responsible. If it doesn’t happen, you’re responsible.”

Accepting the 2016 presidential nomination, Trump said, “Nobody knows the system better than me, which is why I alone can fix it.” But as president, he has often suggested that the solution and blame rest elsewhere.

“The buck stops with everybody,” Trump said in 2019, during a lengthy government shutdown. In 2020, on the same day he declared the COVID-19 pandemic a national emergency, he said, “I don’t take responsibility at all” for a lack of coronavirus testing.

Anslover said Truman took full responsibility for dropping atomic bombs on Japan even though he was not informed that the U.S. was developing such weapons until his predecessor, President Franklin Delano Roosevelt, died.

President Kennedy saw his approval ratings rise after he acknowledged he was to blame for the failed Bay of Pigs invasion in Cuba. President Reagan said he was sorry for any involvement he may have had in the Iran-Contra scandal even while saying he wasn’t sure he was to blame. “The buck stops here with me,” he said then.

At his final news conference in early 2009, President George W. Bush listed a series of mistakes he had made, including failing to find weapons of mass destruction in Iraq. His successor, President Obama, said, “I screwed up,” after his nominee for health chief, Tom Daschle, withdrew because of unpaid back taxes.

Presidents before Trump “really usually take accountability,” Anslover said.

‘We inherited a total catastrophe,’ Trump says

The president acknowledged in a recent Punchbowl interview that voters are angry, but he said they are not mad at him but at congressional Republicans.

Trump believes his party can hold its congressional majorities after November, but he was clear that if Republicans lose, it won’t be his fault — echoing his comments before the 2018 midterms that he would not accept blame if his party lost control of the House, which it did.

Trump’s approval rating on the economy, once seen as among his strongest issues, has fallen throughout his time in office, from 40% in March 2025 to 32% in July, according to Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research polling. About 6 in 10 U.S. adults say Trump’s economic policies have made economic conditions worse, according to Pew Research Center polling.

“The public certainly expects the president to be concerned about, and focused on, making life more affordable,” Republican pollster Frank Luntz said.

Trump instead points to Biden, under whom inflation hit a four-decade peak of 9.1% in 2022 as the pandemic was still roiling the world economy, before declining to 2.7% by November 2024. Last month, pressured by the Iran war, it was 3.4%.

“When we took office, we inherited a total catastrophe,” Trump said at a recent rally, later adding, “I inherited those high prices, just so you understand.”

Andrew Bates, a Democratic strategist and former Biden White House spokesperson, noted that Trump no longer mentions his campaign promise to “immediately end inflation” on Day One.

“He may not remember having made those promises, but swing voters sure as hell do,” Bates said.

Iran and the Reflecting Pool

The president has characterized the Iran war as “a little excursion” or “detour.” To play down how long it has lasted, he frequently notes that U.S. wars in Vietnam and Afghanistan dragged on for years, though the Iran conflict — which he initially said would be over in four or five weeks — is now in its sixth month with no clear end in sight.

Trump has sought to shift blame to the past on the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, falsely suggesting that Biden and Obama spent “hundreds of millions of dollars” trying unsuccessfully to fix it.

But Trump’s main defense claim has been vandalism. And so far at least four cases alleging that, including the most prominent case against an Olympic canoeist, have been dropped due to a lack of evidence.

Anslover said that, after more than a decade in politics, Trump has proved he is not afraid to violate norms of presidential comportment. Lots of his core supporters do not seem bothered.

“For many Americans, it has either been a shift in how they view the presidency, or, like with so many things, they just feel empowered to say, ‘These are my priorities. My priority is not the facts,’” she said.

description:

text:
No one knows exactly how many people have been wrongly detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents since it began its campaign to purge millions of immigrants from the country last year. But the data various groups have collected put the number easily in the thousands.

Now, a force of 22,000 ICE agents, whose training has been repeatedly called into question, is about to get a new brutal weapon: gloves that administer painful electrical shocks with just a touch.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

And if ICE has its way, any abuses of human rights or human dignity its agents commit, with this or any other weapon, will be hidden from the public. That’s because even as ICE is equipping agents with body cameras, it’s signaling that it will release only video that puts the agency in a positive light.

That’s public relations, not public accountability.

Let’s start with the shock devices, or General Low Output Voltage Emitters (GLOVES). Made by Compliant Technologies, they’re marketed as “conducive distraction and deescalation devices.” When activated by a wrist switch, they can deliver up to 380 volts at up to 1.5 amps. A Taser, by comparison, has 50,000 volts, which drops to around 1,200 volts when it makes contact with a body, and a current of around 1.9 milliamps.

The gloves are said to not break or burn the skin, nor immobilize a person, but, as the manual states, are used to inhibit or distract a subject from performing coordinated muscle movements. The company material warns that the technology can cause injury or death, but says the gloves pose “no immediate threat or significant health risk to the general population” when properly used. It recommends against using them on the elderly, small children, pregnant women and severely disabled people.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Given what we know of ICE — agents have regularly failed to exercise restraint or display the discipline required of armed law enforcement officers — this is a tool with high potential for misuse.

Despite the agency’s claims otherwise, ICE has lowered its training standards significantly to accommodate a surge in hiring and a rush to meet the Trump administration’s quotas, said to be 3,000 arrests a day and around 1 million deportations a year. The training period, The Atlantic magazine has reported, was cut from five months to 48 days.

According to various sources, immigration agents have shot more than 41 people since the start of Mr. Trump’s second presidency, and have killed at least 11, including some who were American citizens. In the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis, Department of Homeland Security leaders initially defended the agents, vilified the protesters, mischaracterized the circumstances, and obstructed local and state investigations, which have dragged on for months without a full accounting of what happened. Also among those killed, in July, were two immigrants in Maine and Texas who turned out to not be the targets of the enforcement actions.

While the Trump administration paints undocumented immigrants with a broad fearmongering brush, the numbers don’t bear that out. The Cato Institute has estimated that 73% of detainees have no criminal record, and only 5% have convictions for violent crimes.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

It raises serious questions: Just whom ICE is equipping its agents to shock into submission? And how much public scrutiny of its activities, including use of those gloves, will ICE allow?

The doubt surges even as ICE says it is will deploy body cameras to all its agents by the end of this month. Normally, that would appear to be an encouraging attempt to promote accountability. But ICE’s written policy provides for release of body camera footage after a serious injury or death in custody when ICE determines it to be in the “best interests of the agency.” And if they don’t think it’s in their best interests, the footage could be withheld indefinitely.

ICE claims that the policy is simply intended not to compromise investigations or privacy. To put it mildly, that’s unconvincing coming from an agency whose leaders have frequently rushed to paint those it has harmed or killed as violent criminals or terrorists.

Sign up for the Observation Deck newsletter

Keep up with the latest editorials, commentary and letters to the editor about the issues that matter to you.

Sign up here

Congress — which funded a massive increase in ICE funding for agents and equipment, including all those new cameras — must take note here. Whether they support Mr. Trump’s anti-immigration agenda or not, every senator and representative should demand that ICE, like any law enforcement agency, be accountable to the public, especially when its agents use force in the course of doing their jobs.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

We understand that this can be dangerous work, and that force may sometimes be justified. But the abuse of innocent, nonviolent, defenseless people must be seen for what it is — a crime in itself. No policy should protect that.

And until there are clear signs that ICE is doing a better job of training its agents, it should not put more instruments of brutality at — literally — their fingertips.

text:
We arrive at the Delaney Hall Detention Centre in Newark, New Jersey, on a hot 33-degree day.

There is no greenery to soften the sweltering heat, bar one straggly tree near the entrance.

In these back blocks of Newark's industrial area, large semi-trailers roar past at regular intervals, tooting their horns in loud blasts.

Approximately 800 immigrants, picked up by ICE, the US border control police, are imprisoned inside Delaney Hall, many removed from their children who were born in the United States.

Outside are several groups of protesters who take part in daily vigils, chanting and praying, knowing the inmates inside can hear them through the perimeter fence.

Just near the entrance is a white tent covered in protest signs and colourful flags. It is the 'radical hospitality tent' where nuns, priests and activists from all over New Jersey come to provide comfort, food and toys for the families who are visiting their loved ones inside.

Members of this inter-faith coalition include the Sisters of Charity in New York.

Sister Donna Dodge recently visited the centre.

"Well, at the detention centre there were lines of police people and probably ICE holding guns, preventing people from going any farther," she said.

"So the presence of military-like police people was off-putting, and I can't imagine what it's like even for the families to see that."

When MAGA and pro-ICE protesters turned up that same day, she was shocked by their behaviour.

"These were pro-ICE people and big flags flying and on the flag were pictures of people who had been shot in the head in Minnesota and they were beeping their horns and celebrating the fact that people had been shot by ICE in Minnesota," she said.

Also protesting outside Delaney Detention Centre are the Sisters of Saint Joseph of Peace. Sister Susan Francois says one immigrant was held in solitary confinement here for five months.

"He was in solitary because he needed crutches to walk and that was considered a weapon, and so they kept him in a room," she said.

"Someone who had stage four lung cancer, terminal illness, wanted to go home and die. I think the cruelty, I don't know why other than the fact that it's to break their spirits. There is no explanation for it. It is evil."

Sister Susan believes this lack of empathy for asylum seekers is a worldwide phenomenon.

The headquarters of the Sisters of Charity in New York is only a 40-minute drive from Delaney Hall, so some of the sisters take part in protests and prayer vigils on a regular basis.

They also help fund US passports for the children left behind after their parents are detained by ICE. This allows the children to stay in the US with other family members.

But these nuns have been politically active for decades. Their first protest action was in 1965 in Harlem over voting rights for black Americans. Soon after, seven sisters were arrested during the anti-Vietnam War demonstrations when they lay on the floor of the aisle in St Patrick's Cathedral.

The police dragged them out.

Recently, they have taken part in the NO KINGS rallies against Donald Trump along with thousands of other Americans.

They refer to protests as 'Holy Trouble'.

With the mid-term elections looming in November, the number of raids and arrests by ICE has increased. Deportations are on the rise.

Compass interviewed Sister Kathleen Byrnes during an anti-ICE rally in New York City, protesting the deaths of more than 73 immigrants who have perished in ICE custody.

Sister Donna Dodge says her order is determined to speak out as much as they can. I asked her what she thought of the current Trump administration:

"Horrendous, dictatorial, cruel, only wanting power and money," she replied.

"It's all against the gospel as far as I'm concerned … I have the biggest problem with the Christians and people of other faiths in Congress who are not standing up to what they should know is the right thing because of fear."

Loading...

The final days

The Sisters of Charity in New York have vowed to make the plight of vulnerable immigrants and their children part of their final mission before the order closes or comes to 'fulfilment' as they call it.

In 2023, they made the bold decision to close because they hadn't received any vocations or recruits in the last 25 years.

There are now just 123 sisters left, and the average age is 86. They first moved to Manhattan in 1817 and their founder — Elizabeth Ann Seton — is America's first-born saint.

In 1857, they moved to a 75-acre estate in The Bronx on the Hudson River. This property is under a land trust and will be given to the University of Mount Saint Vincent — a college the sisters founded and currently help fund to the tune of $40 million a year.

The convent is on the same property. The estate is so large that its president, Sister Donna, likes to traverse it in a golf buggy.

The many other ministries — from a farm producing tonnes of food for the needy to social housing blocks in Manhattan — are now part of a plan to transfer much of it to the lay people in the community to ensure they continue on after the Sisters are gone.

Sister Donna says there was no other option for the order but to close.

Sister Donna has watched 94 of her fellow sisters die, but she isn't sad about the next stage in the journey.

"We've had a good life. We've had over 200 years, coming on 210 years of being able to serve the people, especially in New York but other places too. So if you have hope, it's not sad … don't cry because it's over. Smile because it happened, because we have a lot of good stories and a lot of good memories."

text:
The Democratic National Committee (DNC) approved resolutions on Saturday addressing immigration enforcement, with members backing a measure urging lawmakers to abolish U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) while also more strongly approving a separate proposal calling for reforms to the agency.

The vote, conducted during the DNC's summer meeting in Austin, Texas, highlights ongoing internal debates within the party over how to approach immigration policy ahead of this year's midterm elections as President Donald Trump expands deportation efforts.

In July, border czar Tom Homan said ICE was on schedule to set arrest records for a second consecutive month, describing the agency's current enforcement push as "deportation-maxxing."

Read More on News

The resolution calls on Democratic members of Congress to enact legislation dissolving ICE and winding down the immigration detention system. It also calls for restricting Department of Homeland Security (DHS) funding unless certain enforcement activities end, including workplace raids, mass roundups, arrests at courthouses, arrests at ICE check-ins, enforcement actions near schools and houses of worship, and other operations, as well as terminating contracts with private detention providers.

DNC chair Ken Martin emphasized that official party platforms are established every four years at the national convention, while noting that Democrats remain united in opposing the administration's current approach to border and immigration enforcement.

"Our official party positions are determined at the convention every four years in our platform," Martin said in a statement to Newsweek. "However, clearly, the one thing that unites Democrats, regardless of their position on reform versus abolish or whatever other ways to change what's happening, is people believe that what ICE is doing right now and CBP [U.S. Customs and Border Protection] and the federal government should stop. There has to be a better way."

The White House sharply criticized the DNC action, with spokeswoman Lauren Bis telling Newsweek on Saturday:

"Extreme radical Democrats want to abolish ICE and defund the police. Instead of trying to abolish ICE, Democrats should be thanking ICE law enforcement officers for putting their lives on the line to arrest and remove murderers, rapists, pedophiles, and gang members from American communities. Many of these criminals were released from jails by Democrat radical politicians. President Trump's efforts to remove criminal illegal aliens from American communities is already delivering results including the lowest murder rate in 125 years."

Newsweek reached out to ICE for comment.

What the DNC Approved

The resolution details multiple steps regarding immigration enforcement, including:

Passing federal legislation to abolish ICE.

Concluding operations for the agency and the broader detention system.

Conditioning Department of Homeland Security appropriations on reducing detention operations.

Closing detention facilities and terminating private prison contracts.

Releasing immigration detainees except under limited circumstances.

Expanding civil rights oversight and pursuing accountability for official misconduct.

The resolution argues that immigration detention is a civil rather than criminal matter and contends that detained immigrants should generally be allowed to pursue their cases while not being held in custody.

The non-binding vote does not alter official party platform policy for 2028, but it illustrates the distinct approaches favored by various activists and party officials heading into the midterms.

Beyond ICE Reform

The vote reflects how rapidly the party's conversation around ICE has evolved.

Earlier this year, top congressional Democrats stopped short of calling for the agency's elimination while demanding significant reforms.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, both of New York, released a list of proposed changes to ICE operations, including the banning of face coverings for immigration agents, requiring visible identification, restricting enforcement near schools and churches, expanding body-camera requirements and imposing additional use-of-force standards.

Michele Johnson, a DNC member from Louisiana who proposed the measure to abolish ICE, told the Associated Press on Saturday that it’s time for Democrats to take a stand and pointed to the dissolution of ICE’s predecessor agency, the Immigration and Naturalization Service, as a precedent.

“I think one of the reasons why people are not trusting the party is because we sound so academic,” she said. “We sound focus group tested, we sound poll tested because we’re worried about saying the wrong thing or doing the wrong thing and not just like, just stand on business, like take a position.”

However, DNC member Yvonne Reeves-Chong voted against the measure, telling the AP it would only gain support from a part of the party’s base, while drawing “fire” from another group of voters.

“I would strongly suggest we get to the business of winning races so we can make the policies that make a difference,” she said.

The resolution comes as anti-ICE rhetoric has become increasingly common in Democratic primaries across the country, particularly in races where immigration enforcement operations have become high-profile political issues.

Immigration vs. Economy

While many voters express unease with ICE’s conduct and the agency has become a potent flashpoint in Democratic primaries, polling consistently shows that voters remain more focused on the economy, inflation and the cost of living than on immigration.

Public anger over ICE tactics may energize Democratic primary voters and immigrant communities as Democrats seek to reclaim the House and Senate in November, but surveys suggest affordability remains the more dominant concern and that Republicans retain an advantage on immigration and border security, raising questions about whether Democrats risk emphasizing an issue where they are less competitive heading into the general election.

A May 2026 Marquette Law School national survey asked U.S. adults to name the most important issue facing the country.

Inflation and cost of living ranked first at 37 percent, followed by the economy at 19 percent, while immigration and border security trailed far behind at 6 percent. The same poll, conducted with a margin of error of roughly 3 to 4 percentage points, also measured which party voters trust more on key issues. Republicans led Democrats by 19 percentage points on immigration and border security, while Democrats held smaller advantages on inflation and the broader economy.

The Marquette survey also highlights the strategic tension for Democrats. While Trump’s overall approval rating stood at 38 percent, with 62 percent disapproving, his strongest issue remained border security, where 48 percent approved and 52 percent disapproved. On immigration more broadly, he remained underwater but closer to parity, with 44 percent approval and 56 percent disapproval. That suggests that even as his overall standing weakens, immigration remains one of his comparatively strongest political areas.

There is also evidence that ICE itself is still unpopular. A January Marquette poll found 40 percent of adults approved of ICE’s job performance and 60 percent disapproved, with Republicans approving and Democrats and independents opposed. The agency's reputation suffered after federal immigration agents shot and killed two U.S. citizens in Minneapolis during Operation Metro Surge.

Sarah Pierce, director of social policy at Third Way, previously told Newsweek that Democrats risk misjudging voter priorities if immigration dominates their messaging, but cautioned against sidelining the issue altogether.

“Immigration should not be Democrats’ first or only message to voters because it is not their top concern,” she said, adding that “ignoring it is also a mistake.”

Pierce said Democrats “cannot allow Republicans to be the only party offering a vision” on immigration, arguing that criticism of what she described as a “reckless and deadly approach to enforcement” must be paired with “a forward-looking plan for smart, targeted immigration enforcement that keeps communities safe.”

Political Risks Ahead

The debate underscores strategic divisions within the Democratic Party. While progressive advocates argue that aggressive immigration enforcement operations are untenable, some strategists warn that centering campaigns heavily on abolishing ICE could detract from other voter priorities or hand advantages to Republicans on national security issues.

Supporters of the resolution argue that structural changes are necessary to reform an immigration system they view as fundamentally flawed. Critics maintain that eliminating the agency would impair federal enforcement capabilities.

As the Trump administration continues its expanded deportation initiatives, the DNC's action is expected to heighten scrutiny on how individual Democratic candidates position themselves on immigration enforcement.

text:
On August 6 all legal work permits ended, Mass layoffs will occur, leading to Haitians losing their homes. Overnight thousands of legal residents will become “illegal.”

Haitians waiting for hearings will be forced to wear iron monitors, a reminder of slavery.

Haitians, even children, are seen by the government as “the worst of the worst.”

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) moved quickly to end TPS protections, even while the State Department says it is unsafe for anyone to travel to Haiti.

Trump does not care. His hatred for Black people, whether from Africa or their descendants in other countries of the world, is obvious, as is his goal to “Make America White Again.”

Tens of thousands of Syrians living under TPS will also be impacted.

Origins of TPS

Haitians have been covered under Temporary Protected Status in the United States since January 2010, when Haiti was first designated for TPS following the devastating earthquake that struck the country.

As of 2026, many Haitian TPS beneficiaries had been living in the United States under TPS protections for about the past 16 years. The designation was extended and re-designated multiple times in view of Haiti’s ongoing humanitarian, political and security crises.

Soon after taking office, the Trump administration said it rescinded the Biden administration’s TPS extension because it believed TPS was being used far beyond its intended temporary purpose.

The DHS said it was “returning TPS to its original status: temporary.”

The administration contended that repeated extensions allowed increasing numbers of Haitians to qualify for the program over time and described the system as having been “exploited and abused.”

The DHS also said the move was part of President Trump’s broader effort to reverse immigration policies it viewed as encouraging “illegal” immigration.

Critics of the decision — Haitians, as well as human rights and civil libertarian and immigrant rights leaders — argued that Haiti continues to face severe political instability, gang violence and humanitarian challenges, making it unsafe for many people to return.

The Haitian Community

People of Haitian descent in the U.S. number roughly 1.1 to 1.5 million people, depending on the definition and dataset used.

Of Haitian-born immigrants, in 2024 about 70% were naturalized U.S. citizens. With an estimated 852,000 Haitian immigrants, that works out to roughly 585,000 naturalized citizens.

The remainder were generally noncitizens with various statuses, including permanent residents (green card holders), TPS holders, parolees (their order of removal was stayed because of the country’s instability), visa holders, and some undocumented immigrants.

DHS reports that 235,350 Haitians received green cards between 2010 and 2022.

Haitian immigrants and TPS holders are concentrated in a few major areas. South Florida’s Miami-Dade County, North Miami, Little Haiti, Fort Lauderdale and surrounding areas have some of the largest Haitian communities in the country.

In New York City, particularly in Brooklyn including neighborhoods such as Flatbush and East Flatbush, have long-established Haitian populations.

In Massachusetts Boston, Brockton, Randolph and nearby locations, and in New Jersey Newark, Irvington and surrounding areas have substantial Haitian communities.

In Georgia, the Atlanta metropolitan area has a growing Haitian community. Significant populations also live in parts of Connecticut and central Florida.

In Ohio, where Vice President JD Vance is from, he and Trump falsely claimed Haitians in Springfield were killing and eating residents’ cats and dogs.

The Republican governor repudiated those attacks and said Haitians were hard working members of the community.

Imperialist Destruction

What the Trump government is doing, however, is not new. Hostility towards Haitians and Black people has long been a feature of U.S. imperialism. U.S. direct intervention in Haiti dates back more than a century.

The only successful slave revolt took place in Haiti in 1891 against France’s colonial rule. Haiti gained independence in 1804, yet France demanded payments for the loss of slave property; those payments continued for 150 years. Needless to say, freed slaves received no reparations from France.

In the 20th century the United States, the new top imperialist power, took over from France in administering a neo-colonial relationship of exploitation and national oppression. This included a two-decade Marine occupation of the country from 1915-34.

The battle to defend Haitian refugees today is part of the Haitian people’s broader struggle for their freedom.

The Democratic National Committee on Saturday approved a resolution calling on liberal lawmakers to abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement — a move which further intensifies the party's opposition to President Donald Trump and his crack down on illegal immigration.

Newsweek was the first outlet to report the resolution, which aims to not only abolish ICE but completely dismantle the immigration enforcement system currently in place.

The resolution "goes beyond calls for reform" and urges Dem congress members to "enact legislation abolishing ICE, wind down the immigration detention system, restrict Department of Homeland Security (DHS) funding unless certain enforcement activities end, and terminate contracts with private detention providers," Newsweek reported.

DNC Chair Ken Martin seemed like he was attempting to downplay the resolution in a statement shared with the outlet, with Martin noting the party's official positions are solidified every four years at the national convention.

"However, clearly, the one thing that unites Democrats, regardless of their position on reform versus abolish or whatever other ways to change what's happening, is people believe that what ICE is doing right now and CBP and the federal government should stop," Martin continued. "There has to be a better way."

Stopping illegal immigration was one of the key issues which sent Trump back to the White House in 2024.

The president lamented earlier this month his second administration has done such a good job closing the Southern border and keeping illegal immigrants out that the American public has already forgot it was a big problem. Trump said he would have been better off from a political standpoint stretching out his crackdown on illegal immigrants.

"Even my speechwriters, they say, 'sir, nobody wants to hear about the border anymore. You've done it, it's an incredible job you've done, but nobody wants to hear about it,'" Trump said during a White House press conference on August 3. "I should've taken a couple of years to do it."

The president said it would've been a shrewd political move, since the public often has a "two-week memory" when it comes to accomplishments.

But Trump said he had no choice but to completely clamp down on illegal immigration after he inherited "the worst border maybe in world history" from ex-President Joe Biden. The president said Biden allowed 25 million people to illegally flood the USA on his watch.

"There's not a third-world country that would have allowed it to happen, where people [were] coming in from prisons and coming in from mental institutions," Trump said.

The Trump administration announced in July it deported 356,389 illegal immigrants so far in fiscal year 2026, A month earlier, DHS celebrated "zero releases" at the Mexican border over the last year.

Fox News explained zero releases "refers to U.S. border patrol not releasing illegal border crossers into the U.S. interior after apprehension. It does not mean zero illegal crossings or zero apprehensions."

title: US ends TPS for Nepalis: Who is affected, who faces deportation and what options remain
description:
The decision caps more than a year of litigation that repeatedly reversed course before landing, for now, against Nepali TPS holders.
According to official Department of Homeland Security estimates, approximately 12,700 Nepali nationals held TPS status before the phase-out process began.
What happened when Nepali TPS holders and advocacy groups challenged the decision in court?
What have TPS holders and their advocates said in response?
Nepali TPS holders and the organizations representing them have pushed back hard, both in court filings and in public statements.
text:
KATHMANDU: The US Department of Homeland Security has officially confirmed the termination of Temporary Protected Status for Nepal, directing affected individuals to leave the country or face formal deportation proceedings. The announcement lists Nepal among thirteen countries whose TPS designations DHS has now moved to end.

Nepal was first designated for TPS in June 2015 after the 7.8-magnitude earthquake that killed nearly 9,000 people and devastated the country’s infrastructure. The decision caps more than a year of litigation that repeatedly reversed course before landing, for now, against Nepali TPS holders.

What exactly did the US government announce, and when?

The Department of Homeland Security has officially announced the termination of Temporary Protected Status for Nepal, ordering affected individuals to leave the country or face formal deportation proceedings. The announcement, confirmed as of August 15, 2026, is not a new policy decision so much as the practical conclusion of a fight that has run through the courts since the summer of 2025.

DHS published an official notification confirming that TPS terminations are now active across a broad list of designated nations, with a table listing thirteen countries in total: Nepal, Haiti, Syria, Yemen, Afghanistan, Cameroon, Honduras, Nicaragua, Venezuela, South Sudan, Burma, Somalia and Ethiopia. The notification warned affected individuals with terminated status to make immediate arrangements to depart the United States.

For Nepali nationals specifically, this means that the legal fight that had kept their status in limbo for the past several months has effectively concluded in the government’s favour, at least at this stage of the litigation, and that the protections which allowed them to live and work lawfully in the US no longer apply.

How many Nepalis actually hold TPS, and how many will this affect?

According to official Department of Homeland Security estimates, approximately 12,700 Nepali nationals held TPS status before the phase-out process began. Of that group, around 5,500 beneficiaries have successfully adjusted their status to permanent residency over the past decade, meaning they now hold green cards or other independent legal status and are not directly threatened by this termination.

That leaves several thousand Nepalis, roughly the difference between those two figures, who relied solely on TPS for both their right to remain in the country and their employment authorisation document, the card that legally permits them to work.

For this remaining group, the termination is not a paperwork inconvenience; it removes the entire legal basis for staying in the United States unless they can independently qualify for another immigration category, such as family sponsorship, employment-based sponsorship or asylum.

Advocacy groups tracking the broader litigation have previously cited a combined figure of around 60,000 TPS holders across Nepal, Honduras and Nicaragua, the three countries that were bundled together in the main court challenge, underscoring that Nepal’s roughly 12,700 recipients were part of a larger regional case rather than an isolated Nepal-specific action.

What is Temporary Protected Status, and why does it matter here?

Temporary Protected Status is a humanitarian immigration category that allows nationals of designated countries who are already present in the United States to live and work there legally, without fear of removal, because conditions back home, such as armed conflict, environmental disaster or other extraordinary circumstances, make safe return impractical.

It does not grant permanent residency or a path to citizenship on its own; it is meant to be a temporary bridge, reviewed periodically by the Secretary of Homeland Security, who must assess whether the underlying conditions that justified the designation still exist.

In Nepal’s case, the qualifying event was the catastrophic 2015 earthquake, which killed thousands, displaced far more, and severely damaged housing, infrastructure and the broader economy in ways that took years to repair. TPS allowed Nepalis who were already in the US at that time, or who arrived shortly after under the designation’s registration window, to stay and work rather than being forced to return to a country still absorbing the disaster’s aftermath.

Over the following decade, that temporary bridge became, for thousands of families, something closer to a permanent arrangement, since many built careers, bought homes, had children born as US citizens and put down roots that a “temporary” label never quite captured.

When did the current push to end Nepal’s TPS actually begin?

The termination process began in June 2025, when Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem determined that Nepal no longer met the statutory conditions required for a TPS designation, a decision published in the Federal Register that stated there had been notable improvements in the country’s environmental disaster preparedness and reconstruction since the earthquake.

That determination set an effective termination date of August 5, 2025, meaning Nepali TPS holders were given roughly sixty days between the announcement and the date their protections were due to lapse. That transition window was notably shorter than what had historically been standard DHS practice; a federal judge later observed that the agency had inexplicably departed from a pattern, stretching back over two decades, of giving TPS holders at least six months’ notice after a termination announcement before their status actually expired.

What happened when Nepali TPS holders and advocacy groups challenged the decision in court?

On July 7, 2025, the National TPS Alliance, together with individual plaintiffs including Nepali TPS holders, filed suit against the Trump administration in the US District Court for the Northern District of California, arguing that the termination violated the Administrative Procedure Act and was motivated by racial animus rather than a genuine, objective review of country conditions.

The case, formally titled National TPS Alliance et al. v. Noem et al., moved through the court over the following months. On December 31, 2025, District Court Judge Trina L. Thompson issued a 52-page ruling granting the plaintiffs summary judgment, finding that Secretary Noem had made what the judge called a preordained decision to end TPS and had distorted the required conditions-review process to reach a predetermined political outcome.

The court vacated the terminations for Nepal, Honduras and Nicaragua, which had the effect of restoring TPS protections and work authorization for the roughly 60,000 people covered by the case.

Did that ruling actually restore protections for Nepalis, even temporarily?

Yes, for a period of about six weeks. Judge Thompson’s decision found that Secretary Noem had failed to comply with the Administrative Procedure Act, which requires the Department of Homeland Security to genuinely consider country conditions and consult with the State Department before ending a TPS designation, rather than working backward from a decision that had already been made.

National TPS Alliance coordinator Jose Palma said at the time that the ruling brought hope to the TPS community, while cautioning that the government would likely appeal. That caution proved accurate. The Trump administration appealed to the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, and on February 9, 2026, a three-judge panel granted the government’s emergency request to stay the district court’s order while the appeal proceeded, finding that the administration was likely to succeed on the merits, either by showing the lower court lacked jurisdiction over the matter or by prevailing on the underlying arbitrary-and-capricious claim.

That stay effectively reversed the temporary restoration and put Nepali TPS holders back in limbo, this time with the terminations back in force while the underlying legal question remained unresolved.

What role did the Supreme Court play in all of this?

The Supreme Court’s involvement came through a related but separate case, Mullin v. Doe, which dealt primarily with TPS terminations for Haiti and Syria rather than Nepal directly, but which had sweeping consequences for TPS litigation generally. On June 25, 2026, the Supreme Court issued a 6-3 decision siding with the administration’s argument that federal courts lack the authority to second-guess the Secretary of Homeland Security’s core determinations about whether a country still qualifies for TPS.

That ruling overturned lower court orders that had been blocking terminations in several other cases, and legal trackers monitoring the broader TPS landscape have noted that it cleared a path for numerous other terminations, Nepal’s among them, to proceed without further meaningful judicial intervention.

Following the Supreme Court’s ruling, the government pressed forward with implementation across most of the thirteen affected countries, including finalising the practical steps, such as setting expiration dates for existing work permits, that turned Nepal’s terminated status from a contested legal question into an enforced reality.

So where does Nepal’s underlying court case, National TPS Alliance v. Noem, actually stand right now?

As of mid-August 2026, the underlying appeal in National TPS Alliance v. Noem remains technically unresolved at the Ninth Circuit, but the practical effect of the Supreme Court’s June ruling in Mullin v. Doe, combined with the Ninth Circuit’s February stay, has been to allow the termination to take full effect regardless of the district court’s earlier finding that the process was unlawful.

Policy trackers monitoring TPS litigation nationally have grouped Nepal among eleven countries, alongside Afghanistan, Burma, Cameroon, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, South Sudan, Syria, Venezuela and Yemen, where courts have allowed terminations to go into full effect while the underlying legal challenges continue in the background. In practice, this means Nepali TPS holders are living under an active termination even though the legal question of whether that termination was properly conducted has not been finally settled on the merits.

Advocacy groups have continued to argue the case is not over, but for anyone whose status and work authorization have already lapsed, the distinction between “terminated while litigation continues” and “terminated permanently” offers little practical comfort.

What options remain for Nepalis who lose their status?

For Nepalis without another qualifying status, options are narrow but not entirely absent. USCIS guidance directs former TPS holders to its Green Card Eligibility Categories page, which outlines pathways such as family-based sponsorship by a US citizen or permanent resident relative, employment-based sponsorship by a qualifying employer, or asylum for those who can demonstrate a well-founded fear of persecution if returned to Nepal, a considerably higher legal bar than the country-conditions standard that originally justified TPS.

Some individuals with pending applications for other forms of relief may retain limited work authorization tied to those separate applications rather than their now-lapsed TPS. Advocacy organizations working directly with Nepali communities, including groups like Adhikaar in New York, have been urging TPS holders to consult immigration attorneys immediately rather than wait, given how quickly enforcement priorities can shift once a termination takes effect and given that TPS holders who lack any other status become undocumented and lose work authorization the moment their card expires, putting them at risk of detention if encountered by immigration enforcement.

Can Nepalis simply keep working on an expired TPS card?

No. Guidance from immigration support organizations has been explicit that TPS holders will not be able to use expired TPS work permits as proof of ongoing work authorization once the termination takes effect.

Employers who continue employing someone on an expired Employment Authorization Document risk their own legal exposure, which means many Nepali TPS holders are likely to lose their jobs as a direct, immediate consequence of the termination, independent of any separate immigration enforcement action.

The only exception applies to individuals who have separately applied for another form of immigration relief, such as asylum, and who may be able to demonstrate work authorization tied to that pending application rather than to their TPS status. For the majority who relied on TPS alone, the loss of legal work authorization is likely to be the most immediate and disruptive consequence, arriving well before any question of physical removal from the country.

What has the Trump administration said in defending this decision?

Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem has framed the broader campaign to end TPS designations as a matter of restoring the program’s original, narrow purpose. Following the Ninth Circuit’s February ruling allowing the terminations to proceed, Noem’s department issued a statement describing the decision as a win for the rule of law, arguing that under previous administrations TPS had been used as a de facto amnesty program for people who were never meant to receive permanent protection, and asserting that TPS was never designed to be permanent despite having been extended repeatedly for some countries over the course of decades.

The administration’s underlying position on Nepal specifically, as stated in the original June 2025 Federal Register notice, was that the country had made notable improvements in environmental disaster preparedness and reconstruction since the 2015 earthquake, such that there was no longer a disruption of living conditions and Nepal was capable of adequately handling the return of its nationals.

What have TPS holders and their advocates said in response?

Nepali TPS holders and the organizations representing them have pushed back hard, both in court filings and in public statements. Sandhya Lama, a 43-year-old Nepali plaintiff and single mother of three who has lived in the United States since 2008, said during the litigation that TPS had provided her and her children essential humanitarian protection.

National TPS Alliance coordinator Jose Palma described the December 2025 district court ruling as a moment that brought hope to more than 60,000 TPS recipients whose protection had been unlawfully stripped away, while UCLA Center for Immigration Law and Policy co-director Ahilan Arulanantham characterized the pattern of rulings against the administration as consistent with courts across the country finding that the government failed to follow the law in what he called its pursuit of a vendetta against these immigrant communities.

Judge Thompson’s own ruling was notably pointed, stating in its opening that unilateral power has never been American, and that the country has never ignored the importance of humanitarian relief, adding that complying with the Constitution and enforcing the purpose of the TPS statute would strengthen the nation’s economy and unite its society, a striking rebuke that the Ninth Circuit’s subsequent stay ultimately did not disturb on procedural grounds but did not overturn on the merits either.

Is Nepal an isolated case, or part of a larger pattern?

Nepal is one of thirteen countries whose TPS designations the Trump administration has moved to terminate since taking office, a group that collectively covers more than one million people who had been living and working in the US under humanitarian protection.

Research trackers monitoring the issue have noted that, as of the Supreme Court’s June ruling, courts had allowed eleven of those thirteen terminations, including Nepal’s, to take full effect while litigation continues in the background, with only a small number of designations, such as Lebanon, having received an extension rather than a termination.

Pew Research Center analysis published in mid-August 2026 counted Nepal among the countries whose designations have already been ended, alongside Afghanistan, Cameroon, Haiti, Honduras, Myanmar, Nicaragua, South Sudan, Syria, Venezuela and Yemen, underscoring that the Nepal decision reflects a broader administration-wide policy rather than a country-specific judgment made in isolation.

What is the economic and human impact likely to look like on the ground?

Beyond the roughly 12,700 individuals directly affected, the termination is expected to ripple outward into families that include US-citizen children, employers who have relied on TPS holders as part of their workforce, and communities, particularly in parts of New York, where Nepali TPS holders have built visible, organized support networks over the past decade.

Kaiser Family Foundation analysis of the broader TPS rollback has noted that terminated TPS holders also stand to lose access to subsidized health coverage under the Affordable Care Act marketplace starting in January 2027, and Medicare eligibility no later than early January 2027, compounding the loss of work authorization with a parallel loss of healthcare access for a population that was already ineligible for Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program.

For Nepal specifically, remittances sent home by TPS holders working legally in the US have represented a meaningful, if unquantified in this reporting, contribution to household incomes back in Nepal, meaning the termination’s effects are unlikely to remain confined within US borders alone.

What happens next, and is there any realistic path back to protection?

In the near term, the practical reality for Nepali TPS holders without independent status is stark: seek alternative legal status quickly, through family sponsorship, employment sponsorship or asylum, or risk becoming undocumented and losing both the right to work and protection from removal.

Advocacy groups including the National TPS Alliance have continued pursuing the underlying litigation and have signalled they do not consider the fight over, even as the Supreme Court’s June ruling and the Ninth Circuit’s stay have allowed the termination to take practical effect in the meantime. Congress retains the sole authority to grant TPS holders permanent legal status through legislation, something advocacy groups have repeatedly noted even a favourable court outcome cannot accomplish on its own, since a court victory would at most restore TPS itself rather than convert it into something more durable.

The closest legislative precedent came earlier this year, when a bipartisan discharge petition forced a House vote that extended TPS for Haiti, passing by a narrow 224 to 204 margin, showing that legislative relief is possible under the right political conditions but remains the exception rather than the rule.

For Nepali TPS holders watching that precedent, the practical message from immigration attorneys and advocacy groups alike has been consistent: prepare for the loss of status now, while continuing to watch both the courts and Congress for any shift that could change the calculation later.

text:
AUSTIN, Texas — The Democratic National Committee on Saturday voted to approve dueling resolutions affecting U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

One resolution would call to abolish ICE, and one would call to reform it. Both were passed out of committee on Thursday, and the resolutions, which were part of a larger package of resolutions, were sent to the full membership and passed unanimously by voice vote.

For Democrats, the battle over whether “abolish” ICE or “reform” ICE language highlights the intraparty friction between establishment Democrats and far-left insurgents who have energized many party activists in the base that have become a powerful force in the midterm campaigns.

North Carolina DNC member John Verdejo said socialist candidates were beating establishment candidates because some longtime incumbents lost touch with the base.

“Do a better job. Because if you were doing the job that we would like you to do, there’d be no insurgents coming after you,” he told The Washington Times. “All due respect, some of them got fat, while the rest of us were starving.”

The resolution to abolish ICE passed out of committee 25-12 and included a heated debate among the members.

DNC member Marge Hoffa, vice chair of the Minnesota Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party, argued unsuccessfully, “We shouldn’t contradict ourselves by also introducing a resolution that would now call to abolish something that we have a well-established track record of calling to be drastically reformed.”

Despite the additional passage of the “reform” ICE resolution, the Republican National Committee went after the DNC for also adopting the “abolish” ICE resolution, calling it a resolution to “abolish law enforcement.”

“Democrats made it official: they care more about protecting violent illegal aliens than American families,” said Chairman Joe Gruters.

“While President Trump and Republicans are securing our border and standing with law enforcement, Democrats want to let dangerous illegal criminals run wild in our communities. This resolution is political suicide, and Democrats will pay for choosing open borders over public safety, border security, and backing the blue.”

Former DNC Chair Jaime Harrison pushed back hard when asked about whether the DNC has lurched leftward on policy — insisting the party organization is merely an “infrastructure” body focused on winning elections, not setting policy.

“The DNC is not a policy organization. It is a party infrastructure. It focuses on making sure that you have the infrastructure to win elections,” Mr. Harrison told The Washington Times.

“We don’t set policy. We are not a legislative committee. We are not the House. We are not the Senate. We’re not governors.”

But Mr. Harrison himself acknowledged that the DNC does produce a platform, which candidates run under a party banner, and voters are watching closely on flashpoint issues, including immigration enforcement, transgender policy and the Middle East.

“The platform is a platform that the DNC comes up with,” he said.

“The presidential candidate — that platform is what came up because it was a Joe Biden platform in which those are the core beliefs of what a Biden administration would have looked like because it was the Biden delegates who helped to craft that platform before the big switch.”

text:
A federal judge handed the Trump administration a legal victory in its effort to expand its southern border wall, rejecting a request from the Tohono O'odham Nation to halt construction along a 62-mile stretch of the tribe's reservation along the Arizona-Mexico border.

The Tohono O'odham Nation argues the project would damage sacred and culturally significant sites, interfere with religious practices and further separate tribal communities that have long existed on both sides of the international border.

The ruling helps clear the way for the administration to continue its barrier along a portion of the U.S.-Mexico border. President Donald Trump has made border wall construction a centerpiece of his immigration agenda, seeking to expand, reinforce, and construct barriers along the U.S.-Mexico border during both of his terms.

Read More on News

The border wall project has also sparked litigation beyond the Tohono O'odham case. Tribal nations, religious organizations and landowners have challenged various aspects of construction, including a separate eminent domain case involving land near a religious pilgrimage site along the southern border.

Newsweek has reached out to the legal representatives for the plaintiffs and defendants.

What the Court Ruled

U.S. District Judge Richard Leon, who was nominated by President George W. Bush, denied the tribe's request for a preliminary injunction, finding it was “unlikely to succeed on the merits of these claims” that the proposed border wall would unlawfully alter reservation boundaries or constitute trespass on tribal land.

In the order he states, “I conclude that plaintiff is unlikely to succeed on the merits because the federal Roosevelt Reservation exists along the international border and, in any event, plaintiff has not established that construction of a border wall will indeed alter Reservation boundaries.”

In 1907, President Theodore Roosevelt established the Roosevelt Reservation, a 60-foot-wide strip of federal land along much of the U.S.-Mexico border. This came about 10 years before the Tohono O'odham Nation’s modern-day reservation was established, however, the Nation “argues that it had aboriginal title to the land before the creation of the Roosevelt Reservation,” per court filings.

Leon concluded that the government's interests in border security, immigration enforcement and public safety outweighed the harms alleged by the tribe at this stage of the litigation.

“And in any event, I find that the Government’s interests in securing the border, enforcing immigration laws, and ensuring public safety outweigh any surviving irreparable harms at this juncture,” Leon wrote.

He concluded the order, writing, “The international border is an area of great significance to both the United States and to the Nation. While I have concluded that a preliminary injunction is unwarranted, I fully expect the Government in the months ahead to follow through on its guarantees of consultation and cooperation with the Nation to address the Nation's concerns regarding border wall construction!”

The Tohono O’odham Nation's Lawsuit

The tribe has a 2.8-million-acre reservation in Arizona, of which 62 miles go alongside the international border with Mexico. It argues that its “broader aboriginal territory” extends into Mexico, with 17 O’odham communities, approximately 2,000 members, who live in Mexico and “continue to cross the border for sacred pilgrimages and ceremonies at important religious and cultural sites,” according to court filings reviewed by Newsweek. In total, the tribe has around 37,000 members.

The Nation filed a lawsuit against the move in June, including a preliminary injunction halting construction of the border wall, arguing that the proposed border wall will change the reservation boundaries and trespass on the reservation.

In the original complaint, lawyers representing the tribe state, “While the Nation values its close relationship with the Department, it has long opposed construction of a border wall on the Reservation. The Nation understands that construction of the wall would entail significant devastation on the Reservation, including the destruction of mountain peaks sacred to the O’odham.”

They continue: “It would fray the ties between O’odham communities and families on opposite sides of the border, interfere significantly with O’odham religious rituals and practices, and destroy plant and animal resources sacred to the O’odham.”

The Tohono O’odham Nation has worked with the U.S. government for decades on border security, having agreed to construct a vehicle barrier in 2004 along the border. That barrier allowed people to cross. It has also collaborated with the government on a drug trafficking task force, among other initiatives.

The tribe disagreed with the Friday ruling. Tohono O’odham Nation chairman Verlon M. Jose said in a Friday statement, “Too many critical issues were not adequately addressed, such as inevitable impacts construction will have on the Nation’s land and the permanent destruction of sacred sites. The Nation will consider all possible options for moving forward, as this issue is simply too important to the O’odham.”

Impacted Area

The affected area spans a 62-mile section of the Tohono O'odham Nation's reservation along the U.S.-Mexico border. The reservation is in Arizona's Sonoran Desert, an ecologically sensitive region known for unique wildlife and desert vegetation. The desert is the only place the saguaro cactus grows naturally, according to the National Park Service.

In a court filing, the Nation shared a map of the greater ancestral lands which encompass much more than the present-day reservation borders, with land extending past Phoenix, Tucson, and into Mexico.

Why Does the Trump Administration Want the Land?

Immigration enforcement and border security have been central priorities of the Trump administration, with the White House saying that the border wall will be completed by next year.

In July 2025, Congress provided billions of dollars for barriers and other security measures along the border, and the federal government would use some of those funds for the property and construction.

Border wall construction has also drawn challenges from religious groups and landowners. In a separate case, the federal government has sought control of dozens of acres surrounding Mount Cristo Rey, a Catholic pilgrimage site near the U.S.-Mexico border, to facilitate border wall and security projects. The federal government argues the property is needed for border security, while church officials contend the seizure would interfere with religious exercise at a sacred Catholic site.

The Trump administration has begun border wall construction in Big Bend National Park in Texas. The construction may require contractors to blast through part of Mariscal Mountain, a towering limestone ridge inside Big Bend National Park, according to federal maps, environmental groups and House Democrats.

“CBP is building one new access road, improving existing roads, installing detection technology, and placing vehicle barriers in limited, strategic locations. We are not building a 30-foot wall or stadium lighting through Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park, or the Black Gap Wildlife Management Area," CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott told Newsweek earlier this week.

The project has sparked a bipartisan backlash across Texas, uniting local elected officials, environmental groups, former National Park Service leaders and tourism businesses who argue the planned roads, barriers and surveillance infrastructure would damage sensitive desert habitat, alter remote stretches of Big Bend National Park and threaten an economy heavily dependent on outdoor recreation and tourism.

text:
Hundreds of Nebraskans gathered along U.S. 83 south of the McCook ICE detention facility Saturday, marking nearly a year since Gov. Jim Pillen announced the conversion of a state prison into an immigration detention center known informally as the "Cornhusker Clink."

The rally and vigil, titled "We Have Not Forgotten: Road to Solidarity," drew organizers and attendees from across the state — Lincoln, Omaha, Kearney, North Platte and others — many arriving on buses coordinated by ACLU Nebraska. Organizers had expected between 250 and 500 people.

Courtnei Swanson helped lead the event as an organizer with Nebraska Voices, the McCook-based organization involved. For Swanson, the fight over the facility isn't abstract — she worked at what was formerly called the Work Ethic Camp from 2018 to 2020, before it was converted, and has family members who work there today.

Saturday's turnout exceeded what Swanson had expected. She said it spoke to something bigger about the state itself.

"It definitely shows that there are more of us who care than you know," Swanson said. "It's a smaller state, it's a red state, and I didn't think we would have the amount of support that we'd have been shown to have."

That support hasn't been universal. Swanson said she's received pushback for her organizing — including a text from someone unhappy about the protest — though she said it's been minimal overall.

"It does really kind of put you in perspective," she said. "It makes you think, am I doing the right thing? If somebody is this mad about it, is this really the right thing to do? The answer is yes, the answer is yes."

More often, Swanson said, the response in McCook has simply been quiet.

"There has been a lot of indifference," she said. "There are people who are vocal and they dislike the facility, but I have seen a lot of indifference."

The facility's conversion has caused friction closer to home, too. Swanson said her father and one of her aunts still work at the facility, and that she's run into some former workers who stayed on after the transition.

"I have met a couple of people today who have worked out there," she said. "They told me that they just felt so horrible that they couldn't continue to do it."

When asked what the rally's name means to her, Swanson pointed to fading public attention.

"A lot of the coverage and a lot of the support has died down over time," she said, "whether that's from lack of coverage or people just being burnt out. We are still going. We have not forgotten. And we want to show others the same."

Why McCook, why now

The rally is the latest in a yearlong fight over the former McCook Work Ethic Camp, which Pillen and the Department of Homeland Security announced in August 2025 would be converted into an Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facility nicknamed the "Cornhusker Clink."

The facility, which can house up to 300 people, opened to detainees in November 2025 despite a Nebraska Appleseed lawsuit challenging the state's authority to convert and operate it as an ICE detention center.

A Red Willow County judge let the case proceed in October, declining to block state spending on the facility, before dismissing it in March. Nebraska Appleseed has appealed, and the case remains pending.

Since the facility opened, ACLU Nebraska has filed separate federal lawsuits over detainee bond hearings and attorney access, and only five of 49 invited state lawmakers attended a December walkthrough of the site.

A June investigation by Nebraska News Service in partnership with the Midwest Newsroom also found inconsistencies in state financial records tracking the facility's federal funding. The reporting also found the facility has divided McCook, a city of about 7,500 where some residents welcomed the jobs and others say the decision was made without meaningful input.

Mindy Rush Chipman, executive director of ACLU Nebraska, told Nebraska Public Media News the gathering was meant to send a message to elected officials.

"We're here today to send a message to our elected officials that we do not support Nebraska being volunteered to be part of the Trump administration's mass deportation machine," Rush Chipman said. "We're also here today to show our immigrant friends, neighbors, and loved ones that we support them and that they make Nebraska better, and they make our country great."

She pushed back on characterizations of who is being held at the facility.

"There is a false narrative that the McCook facility is going to house the worst of the worst, serious criminals — and that is 100% not true," she said. "Our clients, for the majority, are moms, brothers, sisters. They're workers that we need in our communities. They've been ripped away from their families."

She described her organization's legal strategy as a constant back-and-forth with shifting federal policy.

"It's much like a game of whack-a-mole," she said, "where we figure out a strategy to release people from unlawful immigration, and then all of a sudden a policy or practice changes without precedent, and we're forced to find another legal strategy."

She said a recent Eighth Circuit ruling has made that litigation path more difficult, but that her office is still filing lawsuits attempting to free its clients.

When asked what she wanted Nebraskans to take from the day, Rush Chipman pointed to November's midterms.

"I think one of the most time-sensitive requests that we are making to all of Nebraskans is that it is time to raise your voice at the ballot box," she said. "We're approaching midterms, and we need to send lawmakers a message that we do not support this."

A McCook resident's view

Diane Lyons has watched the fight over the facility unfold from inside McCook — a small, largely conservative city, she told the crowd Saturday.

In the weeks after last August's announcement, she said, rumors spread on local Facebook groups that busloads of armed "instigators" were headed to McCook to disrupt the town's Heritage Days parade. The chamber of commerce director was worried enough to call police for an escort, Lyons said.

When someone online asked who was organizing the buses, another resident blamed "those liberal damn Democrats" — a label Lyons said applied to almost no one she knew in town. She and her husband called around to the few other local Democrats they could think of; no one had organized anything.

"So we figured we were safe," Lyons said. "But everybody at the park was very nervous."

In the end, six protesters showed up — one with ties to a former McCook resident who was upset by what was happening at the facility.

Lyons said the moment marked the start of nearly a year of small, sustained local organizing — organizing McCook hadn't seen in decades. Even now, she said, rumors persist online that outside protesters are bused in for every demonstration.

"So you guys have ruined it today, because you brought the damn bus," Lyons said — a nod to the ACLU-organized buses that carried Saturday's attendees in from across the state.

Lyons said the town's relationship to the facility is more complicated than outsiders might assume.

Before its conversion, she said, the Work Ethic Camp's inmates were a familiar, valued presence in the community — moving heavy museum exhibits, maintaining rural cemeteries, and setting up the town's annual Santa Claus Lane display each December. The facility also employed more than 80 people in stable jobs with good benefits, she said.

"And then all of a sudden it was gone," Lyons said. "The inmates were sent away. The garden was bulldozed. Rows and rows and rows of barbed wire were put up."

Many of those employees who kept their jobs after the conversion have told her privately that they're struggling, she said.

"They don't like what's happened. They don't like the atmosphere," Lyons said. "They certainly don't like a lot of the other ICE employees that have been brought in from out of state to work out there."

She closed with a direct appeal to the crowd to vote in this fall's elections.

"We need a new governor," Lyons said. "Take your frustration, take your worry, take your fear, and take it to the ballot box."

Other community voices

For many attendees, the drive to McCook was personal. A group of University of Nebraska at Kearney students rode one of the ACLU-organized buses, leaving around 8:30 a.m. and stopping in North Platte before arriving shortly after noon.

Ava Lindstrom, a UNK student who has lived in Kearney her whole life, said a restaurant owner she had known for years — a business she had "many memories" of — was detained by ICE and deported in the middle of a semester.

"It just felt really important for me to come here today to try to right that wrong myself," Lindstrom said. "But also just because this is an issue that people should be showing up for."

Lindstrom said she came because she believes the country is failing to guarantee basic rights.

"The fact that we can't give people even basic human rights ... is ridiculous," she said. "I think that there needs to be significant changes, and the only way that we can do that is united as a people."

Emma Risinger, another UNK student, said she came because of what she sees as a disconnect between the state's values and its actions.

"I think so much of the culture of Nebraska is built on loving your neighbor and helping your community," Risinger said. "And I think what's going on is deeply, deeply hypocritical. And I don't think it's right to stay silent about that."

For Risinger, that disconnect is personal. She said she sees more common ground with the people detained at the facility than with the officials responsible for putting them there.

"I and everyone else here has so much more in common with the people who are in that camp than they ever will with the people who put those people there," she said. "So that's why I'm here."

Risinger said she believes a lot of people care about what's happening with ICE, but that campus attitudes vary.

"It's definitely a different culture than what you'd get at UNL," she said. "It's a more conservative campus for sure."

Risinger closed simply: "I love Nebraska. I know we can be better than this."

What's next

Organizers gave no indication Saturday's rally would be the last. Swanson said the event had been in the works for roughly three months, made possible in part by local landowners who allowed the rally to use their property along U.S. 83. She said Nebraska Voices’ ultimate goal is for the facility to close.

Rush Chipman said ACLU Nebraska's legal work at the facility will continue, alongside a broader push to get Nebraskans to the polls this fall.

Gov. Pillen's office and the Nebraska Department of Correctional Services did not respond to requests for comment by the time of publication.
