title: U.S. citizen teens left behind when ICE deported their parents - NBC 5 Dallas-Fort Worth
authors: Scott Friedman, Martha Minjarez, Edward Ayala, Eva Parks
description:
When NBC 5 Investigates first met Dulce and Maria in April, they were living in a Fort Worth apartment complex.
You don't know, you'll never know how stressful and hard life is without them,” Dulce told NBC 5 Investigates.
ICE told NBC 5 Investigates that Burleson Police arrested the girls' mother, Daysi Munoz, for suspected shoplifting.
Their mother told NBC 5 Investigates she repeatedly told ICE she wanted to take the girls with her to Honduras.
In a statement, an ICE Spokesperson told NBC 5 Investigates, “ICE does not separate families.
text:
Two Fort Worth teenagers, suddenly on their own. For nearly a year, 19-year-old Dulce Zepeda has been raising her 13-year-old sister, Maria, in the months since their parents were arrested by ICE and then deported.

When NBC 5 Investigates first met Dulce and Maria in April, they were living in a Fort Worth apartment complex. Dulce, cooking, driving her sister to middle school, working at a local McDonald’s, and selling her mother’s jewelry, she said, to help pay bills.

“You never know whenever is the last hug that you're going to have from your parents. You don't know, you'll never know how stressful and hard life is without them,” Dulce told NBC 5 Investigates.

The girls are U.S. citizens and legally entitled to remain in the country. But some immigration advocates say their case is a stark example of the precarious situations facing thousands of U.S. citizen children whose parents have been detained during the Trump Administration’s immigration crackdown.

Critics said rapid deportations of parents have led to what they describe as a new form of family separation, and they argue recent changes in ICE policy have increased the risk that parents will be deported, even before they are able to make plans for the care of their children.

For Dulce and Maria, their world changed in an instant in August 2025, when the family went back to school shopping at a Walmart in Burleson. ICE told NBC 5 Investigates that Burleson Police arrested the girls' mother, Daysi Munoz, for suspected shoplifting. Burleson Police provided only portions of the police report, saying the case is still under investigation. The report lists suspected stolen items, including a mop, toilet paper and some crab meat.

Munoz told NBC 5 Investigates that she and her husband had just forgotten about some items at the bottom of their cart and then tried to pay. The incident eventually landed them in ICE custody.

The girls said goodbye in the store parking lot.

“Hugged me and told me to take care of my sister, take care of her and she really loved me. And no matter what, just take care of her because she was her little daughter, you know,” Dulce said.

After about 40 days, she said her parents were deported, leaving her to raise her sister. Their mother told NBC 5 Investigates she repeatedly told ICE she wanted to take the girls with her to Honduras. But Munoz said ICE told her that wasn't possible, unless she wanted to spend at least four or five additional months in a detention center. Munoz said she has high blood pressure and feared her health would deteriorate in extended detention.

When NBC 5 Investigates first interviewed the girls, their family was trying to save enough money for a plane ticket for Maria to travel to Honduras, as she desperately missed her mom.

When asked about what she wanted in the future, Maria was clear in her answer: ‘”To go visit my Mom and Dad,” Maria said.

Immigration advocates say thousands of other U.S. citizen children face time apart from their parents and difficult decisions about the future.

“We are leaving children vulnerable in deeply precarious and uncertain situations,” said Zain Lakhani, director of migrant rights and justice at the Women's Refugee Commission, a nonprofit that studies immigration issues.

NBC 5 Investigates analyzed government data from the University of Washington, which was obtained through a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit. It shows that at least 8,889 parents with U.S. citizen children were detained by ICE in just the first seven months of the new Trump Administration. The records make it difficult to determine how many U.S. citizen children those parents had, but they suggest that between 12,000 and 15,000 kids were impacted in seven months.

“Just to put that in context, that means 50 U.S. Citizen children a day experienced the arrest, detention, and potential deportation of one of their parents, 50 a day,” Lakhani said, adding that those kids are now more at risk because she said the Trump administration changed some language in what's called the "ICE detained parents directive." She said that the directive used to require ICE to help parents facilitate plans for their children before deportation. But the new directive requires ICE to facilitate when "operationally feasible."

Lakhani said that this allows ICE to prioritize the need for speedy deportations ahead of arrangements for children, which can result in more parents leaving without their kids.

“So, this is, in my view, very much a new family separation crisis”, Lakhani said.

In a statement, an ICE Spokesperson told NBC 5 Investigates, “ICE does not separate families. Parents are asked if they want to be removed with their children, or ICE will place the children with a safe person the parent designates."

We asked ICE about Dulce and Maria Zepeda, and their mother's claims that ICE would not help reunite her with her children without extended time in detention. The agency did not answer those questions. In a statement, ICE confirmed that agents arrested Munoz in August of last year, referring to her as a 'criminal alien" due to the suspected shoplifting incident.

The statement went on to say, “Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin, criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the United States.”

In recent weeks, Maria's wish finally came true. Almost a year after her parents were apprehended, the family was able to buy a plane ticket and obtain a Honduran visa for Maria to reunite with her parents in a country she had never seen.

“She needs my mom and she already has a whole year with me,” Dulce Zepeda said as her sister prepared to board a plane.

For now, Dulce plans to stay in Fort Worth, trying to build a future alone now, in the country where she was born and raised. The Women's Refugee Commission said situations like Dulce and Maria faced highlight why it's important for child custody issues to be sorted out before a parent is deported. They say if a child is left in the U-S without a legal guardian the process of obtaining visas and plane tickets, or appointing a new guardian, can become harder and extend the time children are apart from their parents.

Data shows the current administration is also deporting people faster. The Deportation Data Project, a nonprofit research group, analyzed government data and found immigrants are now more likely to be deported in less than 60 days than during the previous administration and are less likely to be granted any release on bond.

The Women's Refugee Commission says it has interviewed parents in Honduras who were deported so quickly they had little or no time to make plans for their children.

title: As Seattle sees surge in ICE arrests, residents, advocates on edge
description:
Crowder, 23, had seen videos of immigration arrests on social media and on the news, but never in Seattle.
A growing number of Seattle residents, along with immigrant advocacy groups and researchers, have documented a surge in similar arrests this summer across the city.
“I was not prepared.” Citizens and advocates document arrests Many of the immigration arrests across Seattle so far this summer appeared to follow a similar pattern.
Without warning, several unmarked vehicles block in a car, and federal officers — many with their faces covered — surround the car and arrest the driver.
Those cases represent a fraction of the total because they only include arrests reported to and confirmed by researchers, Godoy said.
text:
Maya Crowder felt horror and disbelief as she watched federal immigration enforcement agents arrest a man at Seattle Center on July 27, just around the corner from where a mass shooting killed three and injured four others the previous day.

Crowder, 23, had seen videos of immigration arrests on social media and on the news, but never in Seattle. Not knowing what else to do, she took two photos and walked away.

More than two weeks later, and amid a reported surge in similar arrests across the city, Crowder struggles to talk about what she saw without crying. She thinks of the shooting victims — but also the faces of children she volunteers to take care of twice a month at Casa Latina and a former classmate’s uncle arrested by federal immigration officers after more than three decades of living in Yakima, her hometown.

She also grieves what it means for Seattle that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers felt emboldened to arrest someone not only in the heart of the city, a day after a mass shooting, but at Seattle Center — a tourist hub meant to connect Seattle to people from around the world, she said.

“I really didn’t think that would happen,” she said Thursday. “It makes me feel more on edge, and that everyone has to live in more of a state of hypervigilance because of this.”

Crowder is not alone.

A growing number of Seattle residents, along with immigrant advocacy groups and researchers, have documented a surge in similar arrests this summer across the city. Many of the videos and photos of nearly a dozen arrests since June show masked agents emerging from unmarked vehicles and arresting a person in broad daylight.

This surge follows President Donald Trump’s pledge to deport the “worst of the worst,” a mission that’s included hiring 12,000 more ICE agents since last July and demanding 2,000 arrests a day across the U.S. earlier this summer.

Local advocates and researchers said this week that arrests in Seattle and across Washington state may only continue increasing, despite some efforts by state officials to quell them. And for the first time, Seattleites who once felt immune to immigration enforcement are preparing for what to do if they see an arrest happen in their neighborhoods.

“We’ve heard of it, but to see it actually unfold — the terror (immigrants) have been fearing,” said Per Johnson, who filmed masked ICE agents arresting a man on Aug. 5 near his Wedgwood neighborhood home. “I was not prepared.”

Citizens and advocates document arrests

Many of the immigration arrests across Seattle so far this summer appeared to follow a similar pattern.

Without warning, several unmarked vehicles block in a car, and federal officers — many with their faces covered — surround the car and arrest the driver. The only public documentation of these arrests typically comes from people who witnessed it and share their footage online.

Such footage exists of federal agents detaining at least 10 people in separate daytime arrests since July 11 in neighborhoods across Seattle, including in Maple Leaf, Sodo, West Seattle, South Lake Union, Queen Anne, Wallingford and Wedgwood and at University Village. The agents were often shown in densely populated and tourist-heavy areas. Groups of officers were seen surrounding a fruit vendor at Alki Beach on July 28 and chasing down and arresting an Amazon delivery driver near the Chinatown International District light rail station on Aug. 8.

Advertising

Information from federal authorities about such arrests is sparse.

A White House data dashboard shows there were 542 immigration arrests in Seattle between Jan. 26, 2025, and May 28, 2026, but does not provide information about individual cases.

An unnamed ICE spokesperson confirmed agents arrested a 24-year-old man from Mexico on July 27 at Seattle Center for overstaying his visa, and not in connection with the mass shooting. But the agency later said it could not confirm details of 10 similar arrests documented in Seattle since June 11.

Facing this dearth of information, local immigration advocates and researchers have stepped in to fill in the gaps.

Arrests often not targeting criminals

The Washington Immigrant Solidarity Network, which operates a statewide “deportation defense hotline,” said the number of Seattle detentions reported to it more than doubled so far this year. There were 36 such reports between January and July compared with 14 during the same period in 2025. All but eight of those detentions reported in Seattle this year happened between May and July, according to data provided Thursday by the organization.

Those numbers are likely an undercount of the actual total, as the data only includes cases reported to the hotline or documented by WAISN members. The majority of arrests confirmed by the organization involve people with no criminal record, the organization’s email read.

These arrests are increasingly happening after traffic stops, a practice “we didn’t see a few years ago,” said Angelina Godoy, director of the University of Washington’s Center for Human Rights.

The group of researchers started studying such arrests last August after noticing more documentation of the incidents — including agents smashing car windows or physically dragging out a driver to arrest them, Godoy said Friday.

Through public disclosure requests, the researchers learned federal immigration agencies often made such arrests after querying Washington drivers’ data through Nlets, a nationwide law enforcement data-sharing platform.

This practice skyrocketed across the state this summer, Godoy said.

Researchers confirmed 50 such arrests between August 2025 and July 3, 2026. There were 90 cases between July 3 and Aug. 7, 2026, Godoy said.

The “overwhelming increase” in arrests was evident in hot spots across King County like White Center, Tukwila, Shoreline and Burien — but increasingly also within Seattle’s city limits. Those cases represent a fraction of the total because they only include arrests reported to and confirmed by researchers, Godoy said.

State officials have tried, but largely failed, to stop federal immigration authorities from using state driver data to facilitate arrests, she said. Earlier this year, state officials said they had blocked ICE and Homeland Security Investigations from accessing state driver data through Nlets. But Godoy said the agencies have likely sidestepped the restriction by using another federal agency’s identification code to access the system.

Such arrests, which have only continued going up in Washington and in Seattle this summer, show no signs of slowing down, Godoy said.

“We’re getting more and more confirmed arrests that fit the same pattern,” Godoy said. “For so much of our state to be going on as business as usual and not waking to the terror on our streets is really disturbing.”

Seattle residents witness ‘heartbreaking’ arrests

Johnson, the Wedgwood resident, was getting his usual cup of coffee at Cafe Javasti before heading to work Aug. 5 when he heard another customer say, “What are those people doing here?”

Looking out the window and across 35th Avenue Northeast, Johnson said he first thought he was looking at police officers doing a typical traffic stop.

Then he saw their masks.

“I knew immediately what was happening,” Johnson, 49, said Thursday.

Johnson, a lifelong Seattle resident who has lived in Wedgwood for 15 years, had fretted over arrests he’d seen on social media and on the news, but he never thought he would see one unfold in Seattle, let alone in Wedgwood. Before Aug. 5, he had never seen ICE agents in person, nor had most of his neighbors, he said.

Upon realizing the agents were from ICE, Johnson said he and everyone else in the coffee shop flooded outside. Some people shouted obscenities at the officers while others, like Johnson, filmed them with their cellphones.

Advertising

“It escalated quickly — people had visceral emotions just at the sight of them,” Johnson said. “(I didn’t) understand at the time what I needed to do.”

Johnson’s footage shows five agents — several wearing masks — and unmarked vehicles surrounding a car parked on the east side of 35th near Northeast 87th Street. One of the officers is shown opening the car door and pulling the driver out by his hand before turning him around and arresting him.

“I’m a DACA,” the man says in the footage, referring to Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, a U.S. policy protecting people from deportation who were brought to the U.S. as children. With his hands behind his back, the man told Johnson and other observers his name is Alberto, his Social Security number and where his family could find his car keys. Then officers drove off with the man in the back seat of one of their unmarked vehicles.

Johnson said he and his neighbors felt wrecked by the experience. They organized a vigil that night in the same location, where people shared information and resources about what to do if another arrest happens nearby. They also discussed how to support Alberto, whom they had learned is a father of three who had lived in the U.S. since 1996 and worked as a painter and contractor, Johnson said.

The neighbors also gathered to grieve, he said, for their shattered sense of safety and for their immigrant neighbors left feeling even more afraid than before.

“It seems insane that it would be happening here,” Johnson said. “But it’s happening in our current day and in our community. And it’s heartbreaking.”

text:
A Windsor man who allegedly posted online comments threatening to kill ICE agents, “the King” and any “secret police” that try to enter his home was arrested Thursday by the FBI on a charge of transmitting threatening interstate communications.

Dwight Pettegrove, 63, was expected to make his initial appearance in federal court Friday in Bangor.

Court documents indicate Pettegrove is charged with one count of transmitting a threatening interstate communication on Jan. 16.

An affidavit filed by FBI Special Agent Bryanna Allaire alleges Pettegrove wrote, “Zi will kill you (Victim A) on site! You will die by my hand!” The information was obtained through a search warrant seeking information from Pettegrove’s accounts with YouTube and Google, its parent company.

The affidavit notes Pettegrove’s post used the victim’s last name, which was removed from the affidavit, and that “Victim A” is a known individual living in the United States.

The affidavit included numerous examples of comments allegedly posted by Pettegrove, mostly as comments on YouTube videos.

On Sept. 28, 2025, Pettegrove allegedly wrote, “Come to my home secret police. Get wherever I am secret police. I will kill secret police anywhere anytime. I’M NOT A KEYBOARD WARRIOR IN THE LEAST. I CAN AND WILL BACK UP MY WORDS.”

On Jan. 14, he allegedly made this comment on a YouTube video: “I do imagine killing ICE pigs. I have no regard for their useless lives anymore than maga maggots, trump and his cabinet. You all must be exterminated.”

Two weeks after that comment, FBI Special Agent Bryanna Allaire, a U.S. Secret Service agent and a deputy from Kennebec County Sheriff’s Office interviewed Pettegrove at his Ridge Road home in Windsor. Pettegrove said he knew why they were there to speak with him, saying it was because of the stuff he puts on Facebook and YouTube, because he says “Kill ICE,” Allaire wrote in her affidavit.

The affidavit states Pettegrove told the authorities in that interview, “that he knows what he says. Pettegrove said that he has had it with them and this takeover and the President. Pettegrove said that he does not have any firearms and does not travel. Pettegrove said he is not out to kill anyone and that people described him as a ‘goofball.'”

Federal prosecutors have also filed a motion to detain Pettegrove without bail until his trial. Alisa Ross, an assistant U.S. attorney said in her motion that his case is eligible for a detention order because he committed a crime of violence, and for the “safety of any other person and the community.”

Court documents state Pettegrove was arrested, apparently by FBI agents. Neighbors to his 560 Ridge Road home reported in social media comments that FBI agents were at the property Thursday morning, including some in what appeared to be an armored vehicle. The road, also known as Route 32, was shut down while they were there, social media comments state.

It appears Pettegrove’s online activities first came to the attention of the FBI in July 2025 when the FBI was sent information from Google that a YouTube user had threatened Google and its employees.

The company reported someone later determined to be Pettegrove posted statements including that he would “kill youtube ceo,” “Youtube will be murdered,” and “You tube must really be taught a lesson, a permanent lesson,” according to the FBI.

An FBI agent interviewed Pettegrove about those posts in July 2025 and Pettegrove acknowledged he made comments regarding Google and YouTube and said he had no plans to carry out an action. He said he had become frustrated over time with his comments being deleted. But he said he was disabled and couldn’t get anywhere and that he did not have the intent or capacity to carry out any threats.

After the agent warned Pettegrove he could get in trouble for threatening people, Pettegrove said he would moderate his comments, and the matter was closed , until the FBI was again notified by Google regarding Pettegrove’s alleged threats to kill people, including ICE agents, prompting the charge he now faces.

Transmitting a threatening interstate communication is punishable by up to five years imprisonment and a fine of up to $250,000.

title: ICE considering buying immigrant detention facilities, other options to maintain capacity in Pa.
description:
As existing detention contracts in certain locations approach expiration, ICE is working to ensure continued access to detention capacity in those areas.
Clearfield County’s five-year contracts with ICE and GEO Group are set to expire in late September.
As for a potential contract between ICE and GEO Group, the warden had no information, Glass said.
“And we’ve heard nothing else.” The warden did not return a request for comment, nor did GEO Group.
Commissioners also approved a services contract with GEO Group, an international company based in Florida that owns and operates correctional and detention facilities around the globe.
text:
This story was produced by the State College regional bureau of Spotlight PA, an independent, nonpartisan newsroom dedicated to investigative and public-service journalism for Pennsylvania. Sign up for Talk of the Town, a newsletter of local stories that dig deep, events, and more from north-central PA, at spotlightpa.org/newsletters/talkofthetown.

By MELISSA PÉREZ-CARRILLO

Spotlight PA State College

CLEARFIELD — In mid-July, ICE published a request for information on “turn-key detention services” for four regions across the country, including central Pennsylvania, where it already has the largest immigration detention facility in the Northeast.

Local activists worry ICE is either trying to contract directly with GEO Group — which owns and operates Moshannon Valley Processing Center — or even potentially buy the facility.

When asked about what the RFI means for Moshannon, an ICE spokesperson told Spotlight PA in an Aug. 10 email that “ICE has access to over 80,000 beds across its entire detention network in a mixture of dedicated and non-dedicated facilities. As existing detention contracts in certain locations approach expiration, ICE is working to ensure continued access to detention capacity in those areas. As part of this effort, ICE is evaluating options, including the potential purchase of turnkey detention facilities where appropriate, or other contracting solutions to support continuity of operations.”

Currently, Clearfield County acts as a middleman between ICE and GEO Group, an arrangement that provides the county government with a “minor” level of oversight over the facility, which has long been accused of physical and psychological abuse, poor healthcare, and inhumane conditions.

Clearfield County’s five-year contracts with ICE and GEO Group are set to expire in late September. The setup offered a workaround to former President Joe Biden’s 2021 executive order banning private federal prisons, which President Donald Trump reversed in 2025.

Activist Tim Smith, who says he has been fighting against immigration detention facilities for 23 years, first alerted commissioners about the RFI in an email on July 13.

Smith was a plaintiff in an October 2021 lawsuit filed by the ACLU of Pennsylvania against the Clearfield County commissioners for failing to comply with the state’s open meetings law in regard to approving contracts with ICE and GEO Group.

“What’s happening now is even more stark than what was happening five years ago,” Smith said during public comment at the July 14 commissioners meeting. “I would hope that today on Bastille Day that we take at least an emergency measure to show your disapproval of what is coming.”

“The [Moshannon] warden talked to us and swears GEO isn’t selling the facility to ICE,” Clearfield County Commissioner Dave Glass told the newsroom in a July 22 email. As for a potential contract between ICE and GEO Group, the warden had no information, Glass said. “And we’ve heard nothing else.”

The warden did not return a request for comment, nor did GEO Group.

However, the company’s founder and CEO George Zoley told shareholders in a second-quarter earnings call last week that GEO Group is “engaged in an active process for the sale of several of our turnkey facilities, subject to mutual agreement on price and our continued management of those facilities under long-term support services contracts.”

He also said that “several other GEO facilities have support services

contracts that expire later this year. ICE has initiated a procurement process

involving four facilities that we hope will result in new long-term support services

contracts being awarded.”

Zoley did not specify during the call which facilities he was referring to for potential sales or renewed contracts.

According to the RFI posting, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security “requires one or more Contractor Owned/Contractor-Operated detention facilities” in the Denver, Miami, Seattle, and Philadelphia “areas of responsibility.”

The Philadelphia AOR — which includes Pennsylvania, Delaware, and West Virginia — facility should have a minimum of 1,800 detention beds and be located within 30 driving miles of State College Regional Airport.

Moshannon Valley has a bed capacity of 1,876 and is a roughly 27-mile drive from the airport.

The airport has become a major hub for ICE flights, with a massive jump from two flights in all of 2025 to 28 in April, 25 in May, and 23 in June, according to data from Human Rights First, a nonprofit that advocates for refugees and immigrants.

The RFI expands potential sites to include turnkey existing facilities, those requiring upgrades, and new constructions, with the caveat that properties must be able to begin housing detainees within 30 days of contract award and only house ICE detainees.

ICE is using the RFI to see what markets have available and how quickly it can ramp up its detention numbers, said César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández, a law professor at Ohio State who specializes in the intersection of criminal and immigration law.

With the lack of transparency, it’s difficult to say whether this RFI is an effort to get ahead of Clearfield’s upcoming contract renewals with ICE and GEO Group, García Hernández told Spotlight PA.

“So often, it’s hard to understand just what they’re doing, nonetheless, why they’re doing it, and the reason for that is that oftentimes they don’t tell us,” he said.

In September 2021, Clearfield County commissioners voted to enter into a five-year intergovernmental service agreement with ICE “to provide detention services for detainees,” according to the agreement.

Commissioners also approved a services contract with GEO Group, an international company based in Florida that owns and operates correctional and detention facilities around the globe. It “requires GEO to perform all duties and accept all responsibilities incumbent upon” the county under its agreement with ICE, according to the contract.

With the contracts ending in September, some community members worry that ICE will cut the county out of the equation rather than renew the arrangement.

For Jasmine Rivera, executive director of the Pennsylvania Immigration Coalition, it doesn’t matter who holds the contract, because the facility is still running, separating families, and incarcerating loved ones.

“It’s always unjust, always abusive, and it’s always unnecessary, regardless of who or how detention centers are being operated,” Rivera told Spotlight PA.

Pennsylvania U.S. Reps. Chris Deluzio, Madeleine Dean, and Summer Lee, all Democrats, wrote letters to ICE and GEO Group last week “to demand answers on GEO’s failure to comply with federal standards of adequate staffing and medical care to detainees, as well as obstruction of congressional oversight,” according to a news release.

Dean conducted a visit to Moshannon Valley Processing Center on June 17. Lee and Deluzio also went to the facility unannounced on May 28, and spoke to pregnant women who said they were receiving poor medical care.

“These failures are not accidental; they are the predictable result of a privatized, for-profit detention business model,” Dean, Deluzio, and Lee wrote in their letter to GEO Group.

Local activists have implored commissioners to take on more oversight at the facility. The intergovernmental agreement allows commissioners to enter the facility with 24-hour notice, but the officials have been denied access in the past, raising concerns about how much oversight they actually have.

“I think we all need to just be very honest that this ‘so-called’ oversight doesn’t prevent abuse,” Rivera said.

“We are the lowest common denominator,” Commissioner Tim Winters said during the July 14 meeting. “We cannot open or close this facility. We have a minor say and a minor oversight.”

At the July 28 commissioners meeting, Winters said there have been no updates to ICE’s and GEO Group’s contract with the county, but that it’s “in process.” Commissioners noted that this is in line with the time frame of the 2021 contract.

“If they offer a contract, we’ll certainly look at it. I’ve already said I’m going to vote no on it,” Glass said during the July 14 meeting.

title: 'Even the nuns are mad': Catholic sisters are standing for Haitians outside ICE offices
description:
BLUE ASH, OHIO — The first Haitian immigrant reported to the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) field office at 7:42 a.m. on Sunday.
The man paused before entering the ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations office.
The group of sisters positioned on the corner in front of the office were from different orders: Sisters of Mercy, Sisters of the Precious Blood, Sisters of Charity and Sisters of Divine Providence.
Haitian immigrants have been reporting to the ICE office in this Cincinnati suburb since.
Sisters Anita Marie and Maria Francine, biological twins with the Sisters of Notre Dame, stood at the door to the ICE office wearing their traditional habits.
text:
This story was originally reported by Amanda Becker of The 19th. Meet Amanda and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy.

BLUE ASH, OHIO — The first Haitian immigrant reported to the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) field office at 7:42 a.m. on Sunday. From the corner, the Catholic sisters watched, their positions on immigration stamped on banners and signs.

Sister Alice Gerdeman’s sign noted that her order, the Sisters of Divine Providence, supports “challenging systems that exclude.” Sister Sandy Howe’s sign read, “Love Your Neighbor, no exceptions.” Sister Patricia Wittberg’s took a more direct approach: “It’s so bad even the NUNS are mad!”

“Where has our conscience gone as a society?” Sister Carren Herring asked as the Haitian man walked toward the field office, where he would reemerge from hours later with a GPS tracker clamped around an ankle.

There would be a dozen or so more like him that day, mostly Springfield-area Haitian residents summoned to report to ICE after the Trump administration ended Temporary Protected Status, or TPS, for the country. The program has allowed hundreds of thousands of Haitians to live and work legally in the United States due to violence and political instability back home.

The man paused before entering the ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations office. At the door, Springfield pastors were offering communion and prayer. He waved to the crowd of nearly 700 lining the street in support.

“ICE does not speak for the people! No neighbor of ours is illegal!” they chanted in early-morning humidity that portended an oppressively hot August day.

The group of sisters positioned on the corner in front of the office were from different orders: Sisters of Mercy, Sisters of the Precious Blood, Sisters of Charity and Sisters of Divine Providence. They are united by their faith and shared ministry, the Ohio Sisters Justice Network, whose banner described the network’s use of “gospel justice” to protect democracy, end human trafficking and support immigrants.

That included advocating that the Trump administration extend TPS for Haitians. Now, it means showing up to support them as immigration enforcement tightens its grip.

“I’ve had people say to me, ‘Sister, they need to come here legally.’ Well, they came here legally,” said Sister Sally Duffy, a Sister of Charity and active participant in the network. She held a handwritten orange sign that read: “Our Immigrant Brothers and Sisters have God given DIGNITY.”

“We are changing the rules,” she continued. “If it was a Bengals football game, and it was the last second on the clock, and the field goal kicker was going to make a 30-yard field goal, and all of a sudden, no, we moved him back, so now it became a 70-yard field goal, there’d be an uproar, an outrage over changing the rules.”

Late last month, ICE started sending letters to Haitians in Springfield, informing them that the Trump administration would begin to enforce the end of TPS for Haiti, a plan greenlit by the Supreme Court. Haitian immigrants have been reporting to the ICE office in this Cincinnati suburb since.

In Springfield, a city of 60,000 about an hour’s drive north of the ICE office, roughly one in four residents are Haitian — and many of them were on TPS. For months, faith-based and secular groups there have marshalled thousands of volunteers to prepare for a potential mass deportation event they fear could result in a humanitarian crisis. Many have wondered what will happen when families are separated: Who will care for the U.S.-born, citizen children who may be left behind?

Now, these volunteers have expanded their efforts to Blue Ash, which has one of the closest ICE offices.

President Donald Trump pledged during his 2024 campaign to undertake the “largest deportation of criminals in the history of America.” He and Vice President JD Vance, who was then a U.S. senator representing Ohio, specifically targeted Haitians living in Springfield, spreading the lie that the legal immigrants were eating their neighbors’ pets. White nationalist groups descended on the city; bomb threats closed area public schools.

The Springfield community watched with trepidation as Trump’s “Operation Metro Surge” wrought havoc on much-larger Minneapolis earlier this year, leading to the deaths of two U.S. citizens, Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good. Organizations working with Haitians in Springfield started stockpiling supplies and forming ICE patrols to prepare for a similar enforcement surge as in Minneapolis — but the surge never arrived.

Gregory Bovino, the commander-at-large of Trump’s Customs and Border Protection, was removed from his position in January after the deaths. Two months later, Markwayne Mullin replaced Kristi Noem as secretary of the Department of Homeland Security. Federal immigration agents dialed down their street presence in Minneapolis amid intense public backlash against the administration’s tactics, prompting a shift in enforcement strategy.

The sisters paid attention.

“They don’t want another Minneapolis … but they’d love for all the Haitians to be deported in secret,” Sister Wittberg said. “I don’t know that we can do anything but witness that this is not a Christian thing to do.”

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson reiterated in an email that TPS was supposed to be temporary, writing: “Every day, DHS is conducting law enforcement activities across the country to keep Americans safe. DHS does not discuss ongoing or future operations.”

Catholic sisters are playing a key role among clergy and other religious leaders who have been organizing demonstrations and vigils at ICE field offices and processing centers in places like Chicago, Pittsburgh and Philadelphia. Religious leaders present in Blue Ash on Sunday also included women serving as a Jewish rabbi, a Baptist minister and a Muslim chaplain.

When Cincinnati-based Ignite Peace, a group founded by Catholic sisters that has since become an interfaith organization, planned the “ICE: We See You” response for Sunday, they encouraged participants to wear “religious garments.” After all, the action would happen on a day and time when many would otherwise be attending religious services.

Sisters Anita Marie and Maria Francine, biological twins with the Sisters of Notre Dame, stood at the door to the ICE office wearing their traditional habits. Pastor Carl Ruby of Springfield’s Central Christian Church and Viles Dorsainvil, a Moravian pastor and founder of Springfield’s Haitian Support Center, offered Haitian immigrants the sacrament before their appointments.

The sisters both said they would typically be praying quietly in their rooms early on a Sunday, ahead of attending Mass.

“And this,” Sister Anita Marie said, “is a type of prayer.”

title: US immigration judges are deporting people in mass hearings – some without notice
description:

text:
A man in line for the elevator bank at the federal immigration court in San Antonio, Texas, on a morning in mid-July told the security guard that he had an attorney. “You’re special,” the guard replied, with genuine surprise.

Upstairs, inside Brittany A Rodriquez’s courtroom, the young judge with stark blond highlights gave an asylum seeker a month-and-a-half to turn around an application for protection or be ordered deported. Another person who told her “I don’t have a lawyer, I only have God” was given until September to find legal representation, or the judge indicated she would move forward with the case regardless.

On Rodriquez’s docket that day was a 49-year-old Cuban man who had his hearing moved up by an entire year, out of the blue; a six-year-old Mexican girl and a three-year-old Cuban boy who may have been appearing in court alone – it was not clear; a 22-year-old Venezuelan woman and her two-year-old son; and dozens of other people whose fates in the United States rested on her decisions.

Rodriquez had been on the bench for only about a month, appointed after a career in immigration enforcement. She and the federal attorney whose role it was to argue against the immigrants – the role she herself had filled for almost six years, up until May – quickly read through a list of people, 15 in total, who had missed their hearings. Now, they could be ordered removed from the US “in absentia”, without being physically present to find out.

Suddenly, Rodriquez found five more no-shows on the list. “I didn’t even do that whole last page,” she said casually. “I think these are all ‘in absentias’, too.”

This quiet yet life-altering scene epitomizes the newest frontier in the second Trump administration’s deportation push, where people are being scheduled for mass hearings in immigration court at the last minute and those who don’t make it are receiving removal orders almost by default.

That, in turn, sets them up for arrest and repatriation whenever they stumble into the midst of immigration agents – or, increasingly, run into local and state law enforcement personnel from departments that are cooperating with federal immigration enforcement, during something as benign as a traffic stop.

“There’s people that are walking around, going about their business, without realizing that they have a removal order on their record,” said Katie Fleming, director of public education and engagement at the Washington DC-based legal non-profit Acacia Center for Justice.

Donald Trump has ranted against due process for immigrants and asylum seekers since his first presidential administration, when he repeatedly complained about their right to defend themselves in immigration court and said the US needed to “get rid of judges”.

“When somebody comes in, we must immediately, with no Judges or Court Cases, bring them back from where they came,” Trump tweeted in 2018, adding the following day: “Hiring many thousands [sic] of judges, and going through a long and complicated legal process, is not the way to go.”

Eight years later, Trump has upended the immigration courts so completely that critics allege many thousands of people are now being denied justice. Adjudicators have taken on roles as so-called deportation judges, while their agency, the executive office for immigration review (EOIR), has become an integral part of the White House’s mass deportation strategy instead of a last defense against wrongful removal.

“They abandon the real mission of the agency, which is to provide fair hearings and due process to as many people as possible, and instead sort of run it as an adjunct of DHS [Department of Homeland Security] enforcement, with the only real objective to be being [able to] enter as many removal orders as you can, as fast as you can,” said Paul Schmidt, a retired immigration judge.

EOIR’s primary responsibility is, in its own words, “to adjudicate immigration cases by fairly, expeditiously, and uniformly interpreting and administering the Nation’s immigration laws”. Yet it falls under the Department of Justice, not the US’s judicial branch, raising serious, chronic concerns about its independence from executive policy priorities, while its nearly 3.2m-case backlog has long caused headaches for both Democratic and Republican administrations.

An unnamed EOIR spokesperson said: “The Executive Office for Immigration Review prioritizes the timely completion of all cases and makes scheduling adjustments as needed to ensure cases do not languish. Unnecessary delay hurts both aliens with meritorious claims and the American public who wish to see aliens with non-meritorious claims removed as quickly as possible. As it continues to add new immigration judges, EOIR will continue to make scheduling adjustments to ensure all cases are handled in a timely and lawful manner.”

Now, the undermining of due process in US immigration courts has come not in one fell swoop, but with a series of policy changes since the start of the second Trump administration that has dramatically eroded the tenets of a fair court system – notice of hearings, transparency, judges’ discretion, meaningful appeals, the opportunity to be heard – seemingly to prioritize speed and the administration’s hard line on immigration, experts said.

The result of these new practices has been to reduce people’s ability to receive individualized determinations based on the merits of their cases, cutting them off instead at earlier stages of the legal process and serving them up for deportation.

“All of these different policy changes and practices and tactics are intertwined, right?” Fleming said. “They’re all part of the same story, which is instead of functioning as an independent court system where there are independent adjudicators evaluating claims one at a time, we’re seeing the courts incorporated into a much broader enforcement strategy.”

Many of the second Trump administration’s policies that have hamstrung access to justice in the immigration courts are occurring at the earliest steps in a case, during what’s called a master calendar hearing. These court dates are often a person’s first few appearances and have typically been mostly administrative, with about 20 cases scheduled at once.

Usually, the judge recounts – and an interpreter at times translates – people’s rights and responsibilities, explains the civil immigration charges against them, asks whether they want time to find a lawyer, gives them a list of free legal organizations, checks that the court has an up-to-date address for them and sometimes confirms the facts in their charging documents – where they’re from and how they entered the US, for instance.

But over the last year-and-a-half, federal officials have debuted tactic after tactic that, as far as critics are concerned, have weaponized these hearings. Last summer, ICE attorneys started asking to dismiss thousands of cases on the spot, so they could immediately place the same people into a more fast-tracked deportation process that often bypasses the judge’s role completely. By January, more streamlined efforts to quickly deny asylum applications without an individualized hearing began to surge, too.

Then, the first signs of a new tool to close as many cases at once came in March, in San Francisco, where master calendar hearings were being scheduled with little time to prepare – a test run for what was to come nationwide, researchers discovered.

By the end of May, they started noticing master calendar hearings across the country scheduled for unusually large numbers of people, with a single judge in a single session on a single day. Notice of the hearings, if given at all, was short and sent out in English; a lot of the people didn’t have attorneys; and many of them were being ordered deported without ever going to court through removal orders in absentia, when they failed to appear.

“These are kind of ways to skirt you getting a final hearing where you can actually present evidence for the relief you’re seeking in immigration court,” said Brandon Marrow, who created bklg.org, and who is researching what the federal government has now labeled “mega master” calendar hearings.

Officials have set a threshold of 100-200 scheduled cases and 150 total people per session for these mega masters, while disproportionately and intentionally singling out those without lawyers. Even hearings that don’t meet the definition for mega masters have often been much larger than they were historically, and at much shorter notice for the respondent.

These accelerated court dates make it harder for people to find lawyers if they don’t already have one, as their timeline shrinks from months or years to mere days. Free representation is difficult to come by, with legal clinics across the country already overwhelmed by their caseloads, while private attorneys require immigrants to have saved up for what often amounts to thousands of dollars in fees.

Ironically, having a lawyer would allow for faster proceedings, Schmidt said.

“If somebody came in with a lawyer, I could probably do a fair master calendar in about two minutes,” he recalled. “It actually took much longer to do hearings, masters, without lawyers if, you know, if you really wanted to give the person a fair opportunity to be heard.”

For the mega masters especially, there are almost always more people scheduled than the number who ultimately attend – which usually means at least some proportion are then being ordered removed in absentia. The number of respondents who are not detained appearing for masters hearings this June rose 28.6% compared with June 2024, while the number of in absentia removal orders soared 183.6%, according to researchers at bklg.org.

“Their case isn’t being heard on any level, and if they filed an application for relief, if they filed an asylum application, if they filed all the evidence – if they’re not in court, the court will deem that application abandoned,” Fleming said.

The reasons why people aren’t attending their hearings are manifold, but two stand out: lack of notice and fear. Schmidt remembers how often mistakes cropped up when he was a judge, where addresses had the wrong street name or city, and where notices were returned to the court instead of reaching their intended recipient.

“The clerical staff was spread pretty thin, and filing change of address forms wasn’t one of their top priorities,” he said. “There’d be stacks of them sitting on credenzas, waiting to be filed, which told you something about the reliability of the system.”

In recent months, the median potential notice period, or lead time immigrants who are not in detention have had ahead of master calendar hearings has plummeted, falling to just 42 days in June. With notifications still sent through the mail, attorneys fear immigrants are not learning of their hearings until it’s too late, a concern supported by existing data.

When Christopher Cusmano, an immigration judge in New York, oversaw a master calendar hearing with 73 people and a median lead time of 169 days, on 27 May, he issued seven removal orders in absentia. A month later, on 25 June, more than three-quarters of the 95 people on his docket, who had a median lead time of just 24 days, received in absentia removal orders, according to data provided by researchers at bklg.org.

In Kansas City, Judge Jayme Salinardi considered two dockets in early June. The first – where 93 people had a median lead time of, at most, 15 days to be alerted that their court date had changed – resulted in 56 in absentia orders. The second, where 96 people had a median lead time of 196 days, ended with just nine, research by bklg.org further found.

Even if people do receive sufficient notice of their hearings, many are terrified to go near an immigration courthouse after arrests there last year. Since at least 1996, both immigration judges and what is now DHS have recognized that the presence of immigration enforcement officers in the courts can have “a chilling effect on the respondent’s ability to present his or her case”. But once the second Trump administration took office, EOIR officials quickly dismissed that shared understanding as “contrary to logic”.

What ensued were high-profile mass arrests, where ICE agents stalked the courts’ hallways for their targets, whom they then hauled to detention centers across the country. A federal judge has since blocked that policy, but enough people had already been affected to sow fear and distrust among immigrants who otherwise would have likely attended their hearings.

In total, judges issued 53,808 removal orders in absentia in June, constituting a majority of overall case completions for that month. More than 13,000 of those removal orders came from master calendar hearings with a hundred or more people scheduled, where the median lead time was 45 days or fewer.

“These absentia numbers are completely unlike anything that’s been seen before in the immigration courts,” said Joseph Gunther, a researcher with bklg.org. “Certainly, compared to before, a lot of things are happening that are completely unprecedented.”

Even if people attend their hearings, courts under pressure to issue removal orders are at times rushing proceedings, experts suggested. In Minnesota, Fleming recently witnessed a judge order a detained person deported because their application had not yet arrived – despite the fact it was written punctually in detention then had been misdirected in the mail.

Once people are ordered deported, reversing course can be a feat, even if the reason is something as obvious as never receiving notice of their court date. Generally, immigrants would have to file what are called motions to reopen, which typically carry a $1,065 filing fee and are “challenging applications,” Fleming explained, adding: “They require evidence and legal argument.”

“It can be very hard to get an attorney to drop everything and represent someone on a complex motion to reopen,” she continued. “So it puts them in a very vulnerable legal position” – one where ICE could arrest and deport them, as quickly as in a single day.

Meanwhile, more than 100 immigration judges have been fired or have resigned or retired since Trump’s second inauguration, many of them being those with higher rates of granting relief or who had experience defending immigrants.

Their replacements have increasingly been recruited by the administration, won over by rhetoric such as: “Apply today to become a deportation judge” who will make decisions that will “define America for generations”.

In June, fewer than 2% of all completed cases across all hearings ended with an immigrant winning relief, such as asylum or another legal pathway through the court.

“When you send out ads recruiting deportation judges, I think you’re probably not going to get people whose primary concern is understanding immigration law or making sure that people are fairly treated or, you know, resisting government overreach,” Schmidt said.

On the same day as Rodriquez’s morning docket in San Antonio, the clerk for another judge at the courthouse, appointed under the first Trump administration, spoke quietly to her colleagues and was overheard by the Guardian saying: “We don’t have that many attorneys” for all the immigrants appearing before them.

Among the lawyers who did attend, many asked for more time to work on their clients’ cases, as at least some of them hadn’t even been able to review the record yet.

That judge, Rifian Newaz, reached the list of no-shows at the court that day and paused for a long time, clearly painstakingly reviewing everyone’s files. One person didn’t get proper notice of the hearing, he said. Another was just a child, whom he then moved to the docket for unaccompanied kids, to give a second chance.

When the hearing concluded, he had still issued 26 new in absentia removal orders.

title: No one should be sent back to Taliban rule - The Hill
authors: Fereshta Abbasi, opinion contributor, Fereshta Abbasi, opinion contributor
description:
Governments are fully aware of this but are still moving toward migration deals and engagement with the Taliban leadership that could send Afghans back into the Taliban nightmare.
Anyone deemed dissenting from Taliban rule, regardless of their gender, lives under the constant threat of arbitrary detention and torture.
On June 22, European Union officials hosted a Taliban delegation in Brussels — for the first time since the 2021 Taliban takeover — to discuss migration and return policies.
But it’s the height of hypocrisy to condemn Taliban abuses in one breath and cooperate in sending people back to them in the next.
Other countries should not normalize engagement with the Taliban without clear and measurable human rights benchmarks.
text:
Nearly five years after the Taliban takeover of Afghanistan in August 2021, one issue should be beyond dispute: Afghanistan is not safe for anyone forcibly returned there. Governments are fully aware of this but are still moving toward migration deals and engagement with the Taliban leadership that could send Afghans back into the Taliban nightmare.

Forcing people back to Afghanistan exposes them to a genuine risk of persecution and dire economic circumstances, while bolstering the global standing of the Taliban authorities who are responsible for crimes against humanity.

Afghanistan today is one of the world’s worst human rights crises — and for women and girls, it is a uniquely devastating one. Afghanistan remains the only country in the world where girls are banned from education beyond sixth grade. Women have been pushed out of public life and face severe restrictions in employment. Anyone deemed dissenting from Taliban rule, regardless of their gender, lives under the constant threat of arbitrary detention and torture.

What is most concerning is not only the brutality inside Afghanistan, but the growing willingness of governments to act as though these realities no longer carry consequences.

On June 22, European Union officials hosted a Taliban delegation in Brussels — for the first time since the 2021 Taliban takeover — to discuss migration and return policies. Germany has already resumed deportations and allows Taliban officials to provide consular services in Berlin and Bonn. Officials in the United Kingdom have signaled that they may be prepared to negotiate with the Taliban over returns, as they watch similar debates unfold elsewhere in Europe.

Reports have surfaced that the U.S. has pressured people evacuated from Afghanistan and stranded in camps in Qatar to choose between forced returns or uncertain relocation elsewhere. The U.S. has already ended the temporary protected status of Afghans inside the country and halted the processing of other categories of protection for them.

The message: Return voluntarily, or we will deport you.

United Nations high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, and the U.N. special rapporteur on Afghanistan, Richard Bennett, have warned against deportations, stressing that returns would violate human rights law and breach the principle of nonrefoulement. The U.N. Refugee Agency said there are substantial obstacles to a “safe and dignified return” to the country.

That principle is simple and foundational: No one should be sent to a place where they face persecution, torture or other serious harm.

The near absence of robust and transparent human rights and humanitarian monitoring inside Afghanistan will also mean that returnees do not or cannot report the truth of their situation. At Human Rights Watch, we have documented cases in which forced returnees have been arbitrarily detained and tortured by the Taliban, as well as the abuses faced by women and girls every day.

A former security officer who had escaped to Pakistan and was then deported back to Afghanistan told me last year that upon his return, the Taliban detained and tortured him for two months.

He said that the Taliban “would cover their faces and beat me every night. Then, they would take me out of my cell, put me in a car and tell me that they were taking me to my ‘death place.’ For two months, every night, I expected to be killed.” He also said that the Taliban had detained and disappeared many of his colleagues. He’s currently living in hiding in Afghanistan.

Afghanistan is not a safe country for returns. Governments cannot pretend that their deportation policy is separate from human rights policy. In fact, most Western governments continue to harshly criticize the Taliban’s human rights record in international forums.

Commendably, the EU led on the establishment by the U.N. Human Rights Council of an investigative mechanism tasked with collecting and preserving evidence of serious abuses in the country. Germany, Netherlands, Australia and Canada are pursuing an initiative to hold the Taliban accountable for their violations of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women.

But it’s the height of hypocrisy to condemn Taliban abuses in one breath and cooperate in sending people back to them in the next. Many of the governments now looking for ways to send Afghans back were deeply involved in Afghanistan for two decades. They cannot wash their hands of the debt of responsibility they owe to Afghans who worked with them or in projects they supported.

Migration deals will take the pressure off the Taliban for their ongoing abuses. This kind of “technical” engagement will send a dangerous message to every abusive government that no range of rights abuses and oppression will stop other countries from making deals with you, even at the expense of those most affected.

Other countries should not normalize engagement with the Taliban without clear and measurable human rights benchmarks. And they should not deport Afghans to a country where persecution is systematic and well documented. The EU, U.K.. U.S. and others considering this path should take stock of this harsh reality and act accordingly: no one should be sent to live in an Afghanistan ruled by the Taliban.

Fereshta Abbasi is the Afghanistan researcher at Human Rights Watch.

title: 'Unending nightmare': LA family details 120 days in ICE detention in Texas
description:
The state department is using that connection to detain the family for more than 120 days.
Maryam and her son were taken to the Dilley detention center in Texas, while her husband is being held at another nearby facility.
Maryam and her son are only able to speak to Eissa over the phone for 10 minutes every two weeks.
After months in detention, the family did offer to voluntarily depart the country, but they were denied "at this time."
If we have reason to believe a green card holder poses a threat to the U.S., the green card will be revoked.
text:
A Los Angeles family spent months in an immigration detention center in Texas, fighting a never-ending battle against the U.S. government — not for something they did, but because of who they're related to.

The mother wrote a letter highlighting what her lawyers are calling "bloodline punishment." They say they haven't seen a case like this where a couple and their son were detained for something that their relative did before any of them were even born.

The husband's mother was a spokesperson for the group that took Americans hostage during the Iran hostage crisis in 1979. The state department is using that connection to detain the family for more than 120 days.

"We are in tremendous pain and have been trapped in an unendurable, unending nightmare," family friend Jacob Hart said, reading a letter written by Maryam Tahmasebi that was published in online magazine The Nation.

"Imagine that you are an independent woman wading through the waters of sexism and patriarchy every day, and then you are told that not only do your own ideas and academic achievements not matter, but you are somehow now responsible for decisions you never made, and for things that happened before you were even born," the letter continued.

Maryam, a professor at Los Angeles Pierce College, her husband Eissa, who is also an educator, and their 16-year-old son — all permanent residents of the U.S. — were detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement in April, and their green cards were revoked.

Maryam and her son were taken to the Dilley detention center in Texas, while her husband is being held at another nearby facility. Maryam and her son are only able to speak to Eissa over the phone for 10 minutes every two weeks.

"What struck me was this seemed to be the first time that the foreign policy ground was being used to target people based not on any conduct of theirs whatsoever, but based solely on family relationship," immigration lawyer and advocate Hassan Ahmad said.

Maryam and Eissa's lawyers say the family was detained because Eissa is the son of a woman, who at 19 years old was a spokesperson for a group of university students who held citizens hostage 47 years ago during the Islamic Revolution.

"At no point has a state department or has the government once offered any evidence that this family poses a viable actual threat to national security," human rights attorney Maria Kari said. "In America, we do not punish people for who they're related to."

But the family's lawyers say this is exactly what is happening, and it appears to have started with an online campaign to get them removed, which got the attention of state officials, including Leo Terrell, who works for the U.S. Department of Justice and tagged Secretary of State Marco Rubio just days before the family was detained.

"All this misinformation, disinformation campaign collectively led to getting the attention of some high-level official at the State Department who then flagged it for the likes of Rubio, resulting in this so-called Rubio determination that they pose a threat to our foreign policy," Kari said.

Loved ones say Eissa and Maryam are hardworking, caring people.

"She teaches all of our classes. There isn't a single subject she won't teach," said Dr. Jennifer Moses, chair of psychology, addiction, study and statistics at Pierce College. "So she just shows up. She shows up for the community. She shows up for her colleagues and shows up for her students."

After months in detention, the family did offer to voluntarily depart the country, but they were denied "at this time."

"She said, 'We love this country, but we understand it doesn't love us back, so that's fine. We're not fighters. We'll go. Just let us go, and they're refusing,'" Ahmad said.

The family says they don't know how much longer they can take living separate and in limbo. The conditions at the detention center, they say, are unbearable.

"There's black mold everywhere. There's bugs everywhere. The water is not potable. I mean, this is now the story of each and every one of these prisons around the country, right?" Kari said. "This is not specific to Dilly, but this is also the story of this young family."

Lawyers say the entire ordeal has been emotionally destabilizing for the couple's teenage son because the detention center is not supposed to house children for this long.

Their son, writing to his attorneys, said that he wishes he could have more contact with his friends.

"He's now been there, I think six times the length of the allowable length, but this is what happens," Ahmad said.

Loved ones and the family's lawyers are now trying to bring attention to what they say is a grave injustice, hoping that if enough people care to write their senators and share this story, then maybe this family and others like them will get the due process they deserve.

"At some point, it has to stop. At some point, there needs to be a line that says, 'OK, we're not going to sink to the level of collective punishment or bloodline punishment,'" Ahmad said. "This is the kind of stuff that happens in countries like Iran."

The Department of Homeland Security sent NBC Los Angeles the following statement regarding this case:

“All detainees have claims heard and receive due process.

“ICE arrested Eissa Seyed Hashemi, his wife Maryam Tahmasebi, and their minor son in Los Angeles, California. Eissa Seyed Hashemi is the son of Masoumeh Ebtekar, an Iranian regime politician who also acted as a spokesperson during the Iran hostage crisis of 1979. ICE law enforcement officers successfully apprehended all three individuals whose presence in the United States posed a clear threat to our national security and foreign policy.

“On September 1, 2014, Hashemi entered the U.S. at the San Francisco International Airport on a F-1 student visa. In 2016, Hashemi, his wife, and son became green card holders. It is a privilege to be granted a green card to live in the United States of America. If we have reason to believe a green card holder poses a threat to the U.S., the green card will be revoked.

“Under President Trump’s leadership, the United States will not be a safe haven for those who threaten our security or undermine our foreign policy.”

name: Policy
title: Shock gloves on immigrants? Trump gifts his deportation goons cowardly new tool
description:
It’s come to this: pain gloves.
The official notice announcing the planned purchase describe the equipment as “a Conductive Distraction and De-escalation Device,” but let’s call it what it is: Pain gloves.
Over $100 million toward “Nonscheduled Chartered Passenger Air Transportation” just for immigrants who choose to self-deport.
So now that pain gloves are on the menu, what’s next for Trump’s deportation deluge?
God knows, Trump must have gotten an advance order of the pain gloves for his itty bitty hands almost two years ago the way he’s been inflicting hurt and ignominy on our country ever since.
text:
It’s come to this: pain gloves.

Just when President Trump’s efforts to deport immigrants his administration deems not the right kind — and you’re deluding yourself if you think it’s all about legality — news came this week that Immigration and Customs Enforcement wants to spend up to $20 million on electrically charged gloves so that its agents can more easily subdue people.

All they got to do is fiddle around on their gloves a la Iron Man to turn them on, place their hands on the local fruit lady or taco guy, and voilà! The person crumbles to the ground and gets hauled off to the hoosegow.

The official notice announcing the planned purchase describe the equipment as “a Conductive Distraction and De-escalation Device,” but let’s call it what it is:

Pain gloves. And: Cowardly.

The malicious mitts are just one item in the shopping cart of a xenophobic spending spree that the Trump administration can indulge in thanks in a new budget for immigration enforcement approved by Congress this June that exceeds the military spending of most countries. In August alone, a toxic alphabet soup of agencies — ICE, CBP, HSI, CIS and others — put out notices that they plan to spend up to $1.8 billion to shore themselves up.

Included in the wish list: $3 million on 9 mm Luger ammunition and $2 million for Glock pistols and accompanying modifications; $1 million for the renovation and rental of indoor firing ranges; $2 million in defibrillators. Over $100 million toward “Nonscheduled Chartered Passenger Air Transportation” just for immigrants who choose to self-deport. Over $300 million for new Border Patrol stations to replace three existing ones in Texas. A five-year contract worth up to $50 million to create Border Patrol propaganda “across various media channels.”

And just in case any of this weighs on the hearts and minds of Border Patrol higher-ups, the agency wants to spend up to $1 million for “four quarterly, five-day wellness workshops” at its headquarters emphasizing “nutrition, sleep hygiene, stress management” and other mental health issues.

May I suggest a workshop on growing a conscience? Maybe one on how not to crash out when protesters or witnesses pull out a phone to shoot video, as is their constitutional right? Or how about a PowerPoint presentation simply called “How Not to Act Like a Goon With a Badge”?

So now that pain gloves are on the menu, what’s next for Trump’s deportation deluge? Uniforms that sprouts porcupine quills at the tug of a collar? Spider-Man web-slinging capabilities? Magneto-type helmets so activists can’t read the minds of la migra? (Actually, that’s kind of happening: ICE wants to spend up to $1 million in helmets for a new tactical team called DAGr, which also wants $1 million to buy night vision goggles.)

“Every decision is made with careful consideration and appropriately reviewed to make sure that any technology ICE utilizes is consistent with all applicable law enforcement policies and standards,” Homeland Security told the Times in justifying the gloves, which its makers caution shouldn’t be used on children, pregnant women or folks with heart conditions. “Our officers are highly trained in de-escalation techniques.”

Excuse me while I collapse — not from some migra man buzzing me with their new toy, but from laughter.

Trump has spent all of his second term trying to equip and fashion immigration agents as a new warrior class, and they have responded accordingly. His wannabe Robocops launch indiscriminate raids, operate detention facilities under conditions out of a Dickens novel and regularly don face masks to hide their identities. They toss out racial slurs to ridicule detainees the way the rest of us use nouns, threaten bystanders with guns for looking at them funny and even arrest American citizens who they think got in their way or they mistook for someone in the country illegally.

But this tyrannical posturing reminds me not of some low-rent X-Men film but rather Syndrome, the villain in the Pixar classic “The Incredibles.”

The dweeb so desperately wanted to be a superhero that he launches a war against real ones in order to turn their powers into weapons he then sells to a gullible public. Syndrome eventually captures the animated film’s titular Mr. Incredible and tells him how he’s going to unleash a monster on a city so Syndrome can save residents and thus earn the public accolades he so desperately wanted to receive.

“I’ll be a bigger hero than you ever were!” Syndrome boasts to Mr. Incredible.

Spoiler alert: He wasn’t. And neither will Trump’s borderlands berzerkers.

Despite more immigrants being arrested in July than any other month in Homeland Security’s history, good Americans refuse to submit to Trump’s roundup reverie. That gets him and his agents mad. The man who orders monuments to himself like a North Korean dictator only thinks he’s a king — or a God — but the cruelty Trump is willing to unleash is all too real.

And, always, beware tyrants who are scared.

That’s why those electrified gloves that ICE want are so telling.

It’s an acknowledgment that agents can’t effectively do their job. It shows how the Trump administration really thinks anyone who opposes them is little better than livestock in need of a cattle prod. It’s a bully confessing that he’s scared.

God knows, Trump must have gotten an advance order of the pain gloves for his itty bitty hands almost two years ago the way he’s been inflicting hurt and ignominy on our country ever since.

It’s the coward’s way. It’s cruel and juvenile. And Americans best take heed of a manchild president and his band of thugs at all levels of government who embody that line from “King Lear”:

“As flies to wanton boys are we to the gods. They kill us for their sport.”

title: The life-altering choices immigrant families are making under Trump's crackdown - CNN

But as immigration enforcement increased, they told CNN they became afraid to go to stores or send their children to school.
